“taccar, kammiyar, kuyavar, matuvaṭippōr, vāttiyakkārar, kūttar mutaliya pala toḻil purivōriruntaṉar. vaṇṭikaḷ, tērkaḷ pōṉṟa vaṟṟaic taccar ceytaṉar. poṟkollar mukkiya toḻilāḷarāka iruntārkaḷ. irāca nikaṇṭu eṉṉum vaṭa moḻi nūl 42 vakaip poṉṉaip paṟṟik kūṟukiṉṟatu. āparaṇaṅkaḷum nāṇayaṅkaḷ cilavum poṉṉāṟ ceyyappaṭṭaṉa. poṉṉōṭu vēṟu ulōkaṅkaḷaik kalantu vēlai ceytal, mulām pūcutal, poṉṉil irattiṉak kaṟ kaḷaip patittal, urai kallaik koṇṭu poṉṉaic cōtittal mutaliyaṉa aṟiyappaṭṭiruntaṉa. irumpu, cempu, īyam, takaram mutaliyavai kīḻāṉa ulōkaṅkaḷākak koḷḷappaṭṭaṉa. tilliyil cantirakupta ṉāl (ki.pi. 5ām nū.) nāṭṭappaṭṭa irumputtūṇ, akkālattil ulōkaṅkaḷai urukkivārkkum toḻil naṉku aṟiyappaṭṭiruntatu eṉpatait terivikkiṉṟatu. potuvāka vīṭṭil payaṉpaṭuttum poruḷkaḷ marattiṉāl ceyyappaṭṭaṉa. paḻaiya vākaṭaṅkaḷil pātaracam kūṟappaṭavillai. atu kauṭaliyar kālattilum aṟiyappaṭa villai. cucurutar kālattil atu aṟiyappaṭṭiruntatu. nilakkīl, malaiyilirukkum nāṉku ulōkaṅkaḷai veyil cūṭēṟac ceyvatāl vaṭiyum kaḷimpu eṉak karutappaṭṭatu. muttu, pavaḻam, irattiṉakkaṟkaḷ eṉpaṉa mikap paḻaṅkālam mutal aṟiyappaṭṭiruntaṉa. vairaṅkaḷ veṭṭic cāṇai piṭittuc cuttañ ceyyappaṭṭaṉa. pōli irattiṉak kaṟkaḷum, iracak kalavaiyaik koṇṭu ceyyappaṭum pōli muttuk kaḷum aṟiyappaṭṭiruntaṉa”.1
ulōka vēlai ceyvōr akkacālaiyar, kammāḷar, aṟivar, ōvar, kaṇṇāḷar, kaṇviṉaiñar, kammiyar, kollar, karumār, taṭṭār, tuvaṭṭar, pulavar, puṉaiyar, vittakar, vittiyar mutaliya peyar kaḷāl aṟiyappaṭṭaṉar. ulōkat tuṇṭai aṭittuc ceyta takaṭu aṭar eṉappaṭṭatu. aṭariṉāl periya ēṉaṅkaḷ ceyyappaṭṭaṉa. caṅkukaḷ aṟuttu vaḷaikaḷākac ceyyappaṭṭaṉa. irattiṉak kaṟkaḷil tuḷaiyiṭuvōr eṉa aṟiyappaṭṭaṉar.
ovvoru kūṭṭattiṉarum paramparait toḻilaiyē ceytu vantārkaḷ. toḻilkaḷil māṟṟamuṇṭākavillai. kūttar, mēḷamaṭip pōr, caṅku ūtuvōr, kampaṅ kūttāṭikaḷ, yāṉai paḻakkuvōr eṉpavarkaḷaip paṟṟi nūlkaḷ kuṟippiṭukiṉṟaṉa. maṉitarukkum vilaṅku kaḷukkum vaittiyam ceyyum maruttuvarum iruntaṉar.
54. āparaṇa alaṅkāraṅkaḷ
āṭavarum makaḷirum palavakai āparaṇaṅkaḷāl tammai alaṅ karittārkaḷ. avarkaḷ tammai alaṅkarittu koṇṭatallāmal tām payaṉpaṭuttum ellāp poruḷkaḷaiyum alaṅkarittārkaḷ. vīṭu kaḷiṉ katavukaḷ, nilaikaḷ, muṟṟaṅkaḷ eṉpaṉavum pala vēlaippāṭu kaḷāl alaṅkarikkappaṭṭaṉa. katti, vāḷ pōṉvaṟṟiṉ piṭikaḷum palavāṟu alaṅkarikkappaṭṭiruntaṉa. makaḷir muṟṟattilum, vīṭṭu vāyililum viyakkattakka aḻakiya kōlaṅkaḷai iṭṭārkaḷ. vīṭṭiṉ cuvarkaḷilum kōyil cuvarkaḷilum maṉattaiyum kaṇṇaiyum kavarum aḻakiya ōviyaṅkaḷ eḻutappaṭṭiruntaṉa. kōyil kaṭṭaṭaṅkaḷilum tērkaḷilum aḻakiya ciṟpaṅkaḷ kāṇappaṭukiṉṟaṉa.
maṇamākāta makaḷir tamatu kūntalai aintu vakaiyākak kōti muṭittārkaḷ. peṇkaḷ neṟṟiyil tilakamiṭṭārkaḷ; talaiyil pala vakaip pūkkaḷaic cūṭiṉārkaḷ; cuṟāmīṉ, valampuric caṅku, piṟai pōṉṟa aṇikalaṉkaḷai aṇintārkaḷ; koṇṭaiyilum kaḻutti lum pū mālaikaḷ aṇintārkaḷ; cantaṉam kuṅkumam mutaliya niṟap poṭikaḷaip payaṉpaṭutti mēṉiyai alaṅkarittārkaḷ; utaṭukaḷukku arakkiṉāl ceyyappaṭṭa cāyam ūṭṭiṉārkaḷ, mārpilum tōḷi lum toyyileṉṉum oruvakaik kuḻampu pūciṉārkaḷ; ataṉ mītu karumpu, pūṅkoṭi eṉpavaṟṟai aḻakupeṟa eḻutiṉārkaḷ; kātil tōṭu aṇintārkaḷ; kālil cilampum, kai viralil mōtiramum araiyil mēkalaiyum aṇintārkaḷ. āṭavarum kuḻai, kaṭakam, taṇṭai mutaliya palavakai aṇikaḷai aṇintārkaḷ. peṇkaḷ aṇinta aṇikaḷ mikap pala. caṅka ilakkiyaṅkaḷilum piṟkāla ilak kiyaṅkaḷilum palavakai aṇivakaikaḷ kūṟappaṭukiṉṟaṉa. aṇital aḻaku ceytalai uṇartta ār, cūṭu, puṉai, pūṇ, milaivēy, mutaliya pala coṟkaḷ kāṇappaṭukiṉṟaṉa. paḻaiya ciṟpaṅkaḷil muṟkāla āṭavar makaḷir aṇinta aṇivakaikaḷ kāṇappaṭukiṉṟaṉa.
piṟkālattum muṟkālattum vaḻaṅkiya aṇivakaikaḷuḷ cila piṉ varuvaṉa: tōṭu, kārōlai, muttumālai, pavaḻa mālai, caṅkili, kuṟaṅku ceṟi, paṭṭikai, cataṅkai, kiṇkiṇi, cilampu, kaḻal, vaḷai, mōtiram, mēkalai, tiruppatam, tirumuṭi, paḷḷit toṅkal, koṟṟakkuṭai, tavaḷa cattiram, poṟpū, tiraḷmaṇi vaṭam, kāṟai, aṭikkāṟai, aṉṉam, kiḷi, cōṉakac ciṭukku, cōṉakac ciṭukkiṉ kūṭu, makuṭam, vāḷi, vaṭukavāḷi, kaṇmalar (nayaṉam), poṭṭu, patakkam, ēkavali, kālvaṭam, kamalam, vāku valayam, tuṭar, tiruppaṭṭi, tirumaṇi vaṭam, kaikkāṟai (puyavaḷai), pātacālam, pattiram, kaṇṭatuṭar (mālai), kokkuvāy (kaḻuttu āparaṇaṅkaḷai ellām cērttup piṭikkumpaṭi aṇiyum caṅkili), kaṭṭakam (pavaḷam patitta kaivaḷai), irattiṉa vaḷaiyal, ciṟu cantam, pācamālai, captacāri, patakkam, kalāvam (patakkattiṉ pakuti), pirapai, kamalam, ceṭi, carappaḷḷi, teyvavutti, valampuric caṅku, pūppāḷai, teṉpalli, kaṭukkaṉ, kaṭakam, caṉṉavīram, utarapantam.
55. poḻutupōkku
aracar perumpālum vēṭṭaiyāṭuvatilum āyutappayiṟci pōrp payiṟcikaḷilum poḻutu pōkkiṉar; yāṉai ēṟṟam kutirai ēṟṟam eṉpaṉavum avarkaḷiṉ poḻutupōkkāka iruntaṉa. pōr vīrar maṟpōr, kuttuc caṇṭai, cilampam, vāṭpōr, viṟpōr mutaliyaṉa purintu poḻutu pōkkiṉar. makaḷir ammāṉai, pantu, kaḻaṅku mutaliya viḷaiyāṭṭukaḷilum, teḷḷēṇam, cāḻal, kōlāṭ ṭam, kuravai, kummi mutaliya āṭalkaḷilum yāḻ vācittal pāṭutal mutaliyavaṟṟilum poḻutupōkkiṉar. potu makkaḷ kāṭaip pōr, kautārip pōr, āṭṭup pōr, yāiṉai ōṭṭam, kutirai ōṭṭam, tērōṭṭam, nāṭṭuk kūttu, kaḻaik kūttu eṉpavaṟṟaip pārttup poḻutu pōkkiṉar. ciṟuvarum ciṟumiyarum ciṟu tērōṭṭiyum, ciṟu paṟai aṟaintum, ciṟṟil puṉaintum, ūcalāṭiyum, vil koṇṭu ampu eytum poḻutu pōkkiṉar. ūcalāṭutal vaḷarntavarkaḷiṉ poḻutupōkkākavum iruntatatu. āyarkula vālipar ēṟu taḻuvip poḻutu pōkkiṉar. ēṟu taḻuvutal eṉpatu callikkaṭṭu eṉpatu pōṉṟatu. mutiyōr tāyam āṭiṉar.
viḻākkaḷ, uṇṭāṭṭukaḷ, kaḷiyāṭṭukaḷ, eṉpaṉavum ciṟanta poḻutu pōkkukaḷāka iruntaṉa. peṇkaḷ cellum tēraiyum yāṉaiyaiyum peṇkaḷ ōṭṭic celvatum akkāla vaḻakkāka iruntatu. āṟṟil putu veḷḷam varum pōtu nīrāṭṭu viḻā eṭukkap paṭṭatu. appoḻutu āṭavarum makaḷirum tērkaḷ, vaṇṭikaḷ, yāṉaikaḷai ūrntu ceṉṟu palavakai āṭamparaṅkaḷōṭu nīrāṭuvar; āṟṟaṅkaraikaḷil iṭappaṭṭuḷḷa kūṭāraṅkaḷuḷ taṅkum pōtu matuvuṇṭum, naṟum paṇṭaṅkaḷaic cuvaittum, āṭiyum pāṭiyum kaḷippar. kārttikai viḻāvil vīṭṭukku viḷakkēṟṟap paṭṭatu. taimātap piṟappil makaḷir viṭiyaṟ kālaiyil nīrāṭi viratamiruntaṉar.
ciṟuvar nellikkāyai vaittu vaṭṭāṭutal, kiṇaṟṟuḷ kutittu nīr aṭiyilirukkum kallai eṭuttu varutal pōṉṟa poḻutu pōkkukaḷ ilakkiyaṅkaḷil kūṟappaṭukiṉṟaṉa. viḻāk kālaṅkaḷil pulavarkaḷ paṭṭi maṇṭapattilēṟit tattam pulamaiyaik kāṭṭum coṟpoḻivāṟṟiṉar. vicaya nakara aracar kālattil araṇmaṉaikkuḷ poḻutupōkku araṅku iruntatu. aracaṉatum araṇmaṉaiyiluḷḷa varkaḷatum poḻutupōkkukkāka vilaṅkukaḷ pōr ceyyumpaṭi viṭappaṭṭaṉa; maṟpōr naṭattappaṭṭaṉa. maṟpōril peṇkaḷum kalantu koṇṭārkaḷ.
56. icai
ovvoru nilattukkum uriya icaikaḷiruntaṉa. kuṟiñci nila makkaḷ kuṟiñcip paṇpāṭiṉārkaḷ1. mullai nila makkaḷ mullaip paṇ pāṭiṉārkaḷ. aḵtu iṉṟu mattiyamāvati eṉa aṟiyappaṭukiṉ ṟatu. marutanila makkaḷ marutap paṇ pāṭiṉārkaḷ. atu iṉṟu kētāram eṉa aṟiyap paṭukiṉṟatu. neytal nilattukkuriya paṇ iṉṟu puṉṉākava rāḷi eṉa aṟiyappaṭukiṉṟatu. pāṭi āṭumpōtu koṭṭappaṭum mēḷaṅkaḷ iruntaṉa. vevvēṟu ōcaikaḷai eḻuppum paṟaikaḷ vevvēṟu ceyal puriyum kālaṅkaḷil koṭṭappaṭṭaṉa. nirai kavarumpōtu koṭṭappaṭuvatu ēṟu kōṭ paṟai. veṟiyāṭumpōtu olikkappaṭum paṟai murukiyam. maṇak kālattil muḻakkappaṭuvatu maṇamuḻavu. tēriḻukkum pōtu koṭṭappaṭuvatu tērōṭṭup paṟai. nellaṟukkum pōtu aṟaiyil pāṭuvatu nellarikiṇai. aracaṉ veḷiyē puṟappaṭum pōtu taṭṭappaṭuvatu puṟappāṭṭup paṟai. mīṉ piṭikkac cellumpōtu koṭṭappaṭuvatu mīṉ kōṭ paṟai. cūṟaiyāṭum pōtu koṭṭappaṭuvatu cūṟai kōṭpaṟai.
pōrkkālattu yāṉai kutirai kālāṭ paṭaikaḷukku ūkka mūṭṭum poruṭṭup palvakai vāttiyaṅkaḷ olikkappaṭṭaṉa. avai iyam, icaik karuvi, vāttiyam, vācciyam eṉappaṭṭaṉa. ivai tōṟ karuvi, tuḷaik karuvi, narampuk karuvi, kañcak karuvi eṉa nālvakaip paṭṭaṉa. tamiḻukkuriya ēḻicaikaḷ kural, tuttam, kaikkiḷai, uḻai, iḷi, viḷari, tāram eṉpaṉa. ivaikkuriya eḻuttukkaḷ ā mutaliya neṭil ēḻum. ca, ri, ka, ma, pa, ta, ni eṉṉum eḻuttukkaḷ piṟkālattil vaḻakkukku vantaṉa. mūṅkil, koṉṟaip paḻattaṉi kōtu, āmpaṟ ṟaṇṭu, maram mutaliyavaṟṟil ceyyappaṭṭa kuḻalkaḷiruntaṉa. ekkāḷa vakaikaḷil tārai, kāḷam, kākaḷam, ammiyam, ciṉṉam eṉpaṉavum kompu vakaikaḷil kōṭu, iralai, vayir mutaliyaṉavum iruntaṉa.
narampuk karuvikaḷil ciṟappuṭaiyatu yāḻ. avaikaḷukku ēḻu, irupattoṉṟu allatu ataṟku mēṟpaṭṭa narampukaḷ iruntaṉa. paṟai, muracu, pērikai, mattaḷam, ākuḷi, ellari, callikai, kiṇai mutaliyaṉa mēḷa vakaikaḷuḷ cila. iṉṟu, ilaṅkait tīvil eḻupatukku mēṟpaṭṭa mēḷa vakaikaḷ vaḻaṅkukiṉṟaṉa. itaṉāl akkālattil palavakai mēḷaṅkaḷ iruntaṉaveṉṟu aṟiya varukiṟatu. pāṇar kaiyil koṇṭu tirintu aṭittup pāṭum ciṟiya mēḷaṅkaḷ tārai, uṭukkai mutaliyaṉa.
tamiḻar nūlkaḷaip pāṭal vaṭivil ceytu icaiyōṭu pāṭi vantaṉar. āṭalkaḷōṭu pāṭalkaḷum pāṭappaṭṭaṉa. peṇkaḷ, iḻavuk kālattil tamatu tukkattai oppāri eṉṉum pāṭalkaḷākap pāṭiṉar.
“pantāṭuvatilum pāṭṭu, ūcalāṭuvatilum pāṭṭu, neṟkuṟṟu vatilum pāṭṭu, uḻavilum pāṭṭu, pōrilum pāṭṭu tamiḻariṭaiyē malintu kāṇap paṭum. tamiḻarkku aḻukaiyum pāṭṭāy varum. maṇamum pāṭṭāy nikaḻum. toḻukaiyum pāṭṭāl viḷaṅkum. tamiḻar tey vattaippāṭṭum icaiyum payilavē vaṇaṅkuvar. ēṟṟap pāṭṭu, kappaṟ pāṭṭu, iṟavaippāṭṭu, paḷḷi yeḻuccippāṭṭu, tālāṭṭuppāṭṭu, pāvaippāṭṭu, maṟattiyarpāṭṭu, kuṟattiyarpāṭṭu, irēkaippāṭṭu, kuṟippāṭṭu, paḷḷuppāṭṭu, paṟaippāṭṭu, vaḷḷuvarpāṭṭu, vaṇṭip pāṭṭu, ammāṉaippāṭṭu, kaḻaṅkup pāṭṭu, pallāṅkuḻippāṭṭu, tōḻippāṭṭu, pāṇṭippāṭṭu, kaṭai tiṟappuppāṭṭu, cintuppāṭṭu, cantappāṭṭu, piḷḷaippāṭṭu, koḷḷaippāṭṭu, kaḷḷarpāṭṭu, veṟṟippāṭṭu, vāḻttuppāṭṭu, maṅkalappāṭṭu, maṇappāṭṭu, kātaṟpāṭṭu, kāvaṭippāṭṭu, pakaṭurappaṟpāṭṭu, iṭaiyarpāṭṭu, vēṭuvarpāṭṭu, naṭaippāṭṭu, kummippāṭṭu, kuravaippāṭṭu, kaivīcaṟpāṭṭu, cappāṇippāṭṭu, kīraippāṭṭu, kōlappāṭṭu, kōlaṭippāṭṭu, cilampappāṭṭu, villuppāṭṭu, talluppāṭṭu (oruvarp pāṭa etirttup pāṭum pāṭṭu - malai nāṭṭu vaḻakku), kōyil pāṭṭu, kuḻaṟpāṭṭu, kūttiṟ pāṭṭu mutaliya icaip pāṭṭukaḷ ellām tamiḻaruṭaiyavai”.
muṟkālattil icai vaḷartta kuṭumpattār pāṇar eṉa aṟiyap paṭṭaṉar. akkālattilirunta icai aṟiñar tuḷaik karuvivācip pōr, tōṟkaruvi vācippōr, narampuk karuvi vācippōr, kaṇṭat tāṟ pāṭuvōr eṉa nālvakaip piriviṉarāka amaintu icai vaḷart tārkaḷ. tirunīlakaṇṭa yāḻppāṇar vācitta yāḻ cakōṭa yāḻ. tēvāra tiruvācakaṅkaḷ akkālattil ciṟanta icaippāṭalkaḷāka viḷaṅkiṉa. cōḻa nāṭṭil uṟaiyūril tōṉṟiya tiruppaṇṇāḻvār tiruvaraṅkak kaṭavuḷukku icait tamiḻt toṇṭu ceytu perumpēṟu peṟṟār. tiruttoṇṭar purāṇattil kūṟappaṭum āṉāyaṉār vēyṅkuḻalil iṟaivaṉiṉ ainteḻuttai icaic curaṅkaḷākak koṇṭu vācittu iṟaivaṉaruḷ peṟṟār. aruṇakiri nātar pāṭiya pākkaḷ canta icai yil ciṟantavai. tirumuṟai kaṇṭa cōḻaṉ, tirunīlakaṇṭa yāḻppāṇar marapil vanta pāṭiṉiyāraik koṇṭu tēvāraṅkaḷukkup paṇṇamaiti yiṉai vakuttamaittāṉ. cēntaṉār mutaliya oṉpatiṉmarāṟ pāṭap peṟṟa pāṭalkaḷ tēvārattai oppap paṇṇaṭaivu peṟṟuḷḷaṉa. irācarāca cōḻaṉ tēvārat tiruppatikam pāṭutaṟkum icai pāṭutaṟ kum palarait tañcaip periya kōyilil niyamittāṉ. muttut tāṇṭa var kīrttaṉai, irāma nāṭakak kīrttaṉai mutaliyaṉa piṟkāla icaip pāṭalkaḷākum. yāḻum vīṇaiyum iruvēṟu icaik karuvikaḷ.
icaiyiṉ kālattai aḷappataṟkut tāḷam vaḻakkil iruntatu. tāḷattaip paṟṟik kūṟum tāḷa ōttu, tāḷa camuttiram mutaliya nūlkaḷ iruntaṉa. icaiyaip paṟṟik kūṟum icai nuṇukkam, mutu nārai, mutu kuruku, intira kāḷiyam, pañcamarapu, parata cēṉāpatiyam mutaliya pala nūlkaḷ iruntaṉa. ivai ippoḻutu iṟantu viṭṭaṉa.
57. pōr
tamiḻaracar perumpālum tamatu āṇaiyaip piṟa aracar mītu celuttum poruṭṭup pōr ceytaṉar. pōr perumpālum aṟuppuk kālattiṉ piṉ nikaḻntatu. mēṟkoḷḷappaṭṭa pōrkaḷiṉ taṉmai nōkki avai veṭci, vañci, uḻiñai, tumpai, vākai eṉap peyar peṟṟaṉa. pōr vīrar avvak kālattil muṭiyil cūṭik koṇṭa pūkkaḷ kāraṇamāka appeyarkaḷ tōṉṟiṉa. tamiḻnāṭṭai āṇṭa mūvēntarukkum vevvēṟu pūkkaḷ iruntaṉa. pāṇṭiyaṉukku vēppam pūvum, cōḻaṉukku āttip pūvum cēraṉukkup paṉaṅkuruttum aṭaiyāḷap pūkkaḷākum. iv varacarkaḷiṉ paṭai vīrar tammaracariṉ pūvaic cūṭutal marapu. cila camayaṅkaḷil avarkaḷ ap pūkkaḷaip poṉṉiṉāl ceytu cūṭiṉar. veṭci eṉpatu oru aracaṉ māṟṟāṉuṭaiya pacuk kūṭṭaṅ kaḷaik kavartal. pacukkaḷai mīṭṭal karantai eṉa aṟiyappaṭum. vañci, māṟṟāṉ mītu paṭai eṭuttuc cellutal. uḻiñai, ōr aracaṉ iṉ ṉoru aracaṉiṉ kōṭṭaiyai muṟṟukaiyiṭutal. tumpai, iru paṭai kaḷum oṉṟai oṉṟu etirttup porutal. vākai, veṟṟiyaik kuṟikkum. kāñci, ulaka nilaiyāmaiyaik kūṟuvatu. pāṭāṇ, aracar peru makkaḷiṉ veṟṟiyaiyum pukaḻaiyum pulavarkaḷ pāṭuvatu. muṟkālap pōrkaḷ vīram, tiṟamai, valimai mutaliyavaṟṟaik kāṭṭutaṟkuc ceyyap paṭṭamaiyāl avai aracariṉ poḻutu pōkkukaḷākavum iruntaṉa. 
pōrkkaḷam, kaḷari, paṟantalai, mutunilam eṉa aṟiyappaṭṭatu. paṭaikaḷ aṇi, uṇṭai, oṭṭu mutaliya pala pirivukaḷākap pirikkap paṭṭiruntaṉa. muṉṉaṇi, ākkam, koṭippaṭai, tār, tūci, niraip paṭai eṉappaṭṭatu. piṉ paṭai kūḻai eṉappaṭṭatu. yāṉai, tēr, kutirai, kālāḷ eṉap paṭai nālvakaip paṭṭiruntatu. yāṉai vīraṉ pulittōl kavacam aṇintu ceṉṟāṉ. avaṉaic cūḻntu cila vīrar ceṉṟaṉar. yāṉai pākaṉāl naṉku paḻakkappaṭṭiruntatu. atu kantu allatu taṟiyil kaṭṭappaṭṭatu. ataṟku ariciyum carkkaraiyum kalanta cōṟṟuk kavaḷam koṭukkappaṭṭatu. ataṟku nīrāṭṭik kuṅkumam pūci neṟṟippaṭṭaṅ kaṭṭappaṭṭatu. cūḻi, ōṭai eṉpaṉa neṟṟip paṭṭattaik kuṟikkum peyarkaḷ.
tērkaḷ niṟamūṭṭiya tuṇikaḷālum, pūmālaikaḷ, ilaikaḷā lum alaṅkarikkappaṭṭaṉa. avai nirai niraiyākap pōrkkaḷattukkuc ceṉṟaṉa. pōril vil, ampu, vaḷaitaṭi, īṭṭi, vēl, vāḷ pōṉṟa āyutaṅkaḷ payaṉpaṭuttappaṭṭaṉa. taṭi, taṇṭu, eṟuḻ, kuṇil mutaliyaṉa taṇṭu vakaikaḷil cila. vil, kokkarai, cilai, taṭi, tavar, muṉi, koṭu maram mutaliyaṉa vil vakaikaḷil cila. vāḷ, uvaṇi, ēṟi, kaṭuttalai, tuvaṭṭi, navir, nāṭṭam, vañcam, cuṟumpiṭi, curikai, mutaliyaṉa īṭṭi vakaiyil cila. vēl, eyil, araṇam, eḵkam, kuntam, ñāṅkar, uṭampiṭi, viṭṭēṟu mutaliyaṉa vēlvakaiyuḷ cila. ampu, kaṇai, katiram, kō, kōl, toṭai, tōṇi, pakaḻi, paḷḷam, puṭai, vaṇṭu, vāḷi mutaliyaṉa ampu vakaiyuḷ cila. nāṇi, nāṇ, pūram, āvam, koṭai, nāri, narampu, pūṭṭu, uṭu mutaliyaṉa vil nāṇiṉ peyarkaḷ. kēṭakam, kiṭuku, kaṭakam, taṭṭu, paricai, palakai, maṟai, vaṭṭaṇam, vaṭṭam, tōl, tōṟparam mutaliyaṉa paricai vakaiyuḷ cila. mēlakam, araṇi, ācu, kantaḷam, mey yuṟai eṉpaṉa kavaca vakaikaḷuḷ cila. kaik kavacam kaippuṭai eṉap paṭṭatu. aracaṉiṭattil pōr muracu iruntatu. atu nīrāṭṭi, neṟkati rāl alaṅkarittu uyirp paliyiṭṭu vaḻipaṭappaṭṭatu. māṟṟaracaṉiṉ kāval marattai veṭṭit tuṇṭāṭi ataṉāl pōr muracu ceyyap paṭṭatu.
pōril iṟappōr vīra corkkam celkiṟārkaḷ eṉa makkaḷ nampiṉārkaḷ. pōril iṟavātu mutumai aṭaintu allatu nōy vāyppaṭṭu iṟakkum aracariṉ uṭalait taruppaiyil kiṭattivāḷāl pōḻntu piṉ cuṭuvatu allatu nallaṭakkam ceyvatu akkāla vaḻak kāka iruntatu. pōr toṭaṅkum muṉ antaṇar, peṇkaḷ, nōyā ḷar, vayōtikar, ciṟuvar eṉpōrai appuṟappaṭuttumpaṭi pakaivar muṉṉaṟivippuc ceyvar.
otta paṭaik kalaṅkaḷillātavaṉuṭaṉ pōr ceyvatu, tōṟ ṟōṭuvōṉ, kuṭumi kulaintōṉ, tūtar mutalāṉōraik kolvatu nītikku māṟu eṉak koḷḷappaṭṭatu. pōril kāyampaṭṭavarkaḷ palakaiyil vaittu eṭuttuc cellappaṭṭārkaḷ. kāyaṅkaḷ ūciyi ṉāl taikkappaṭṭaṉa. avvūci neṭu veḷḷūci eṉa aṟiyappaṭṭatu. pōril vīram kāṭṭiyavarkaḷukku aracaṉ paṭṭaṅkaḷ vaḻaṅkiṉāṉ. paṭait talaivaṉ ēṉātip paṭṭattukku aṭaiyāḷamāka mōtiram vaḻaṅkappaṭṭatu. veṉṟa aracaṉ tōṟṟa aracaṉiṉ muṭiyai urukkiya poṉṉāl vīra taṇṭai allatu mālai ceytu aṇintāṉ. veṟṟi peṟṟa aracaṉ mālai ceytu aṇintāṉ. veṟṟi peṟṟa aracaṉ tōṟṟa aracaṉiṉ nīrt tuṟaiyil taṉatu koṟṟak kuṭaiyai nīrāṭṭu talum avaṉuṭaiya kāval marattil taṉatu yāṉaiyaik kaṭṭutalum ciṟanta ceyalkaḷākak karutappaṭṭaṉa.
58. paṭai
mūlap paṭai, kūlip paṭai, naṭpup paṭai, pakaip paṭai, nāṭṭup paṭai, vēṭṭuvap paṭai eṉap paṭaikaḷ aṟu vakaiyiṉa. talaimuṟai yāka aracaṉiṭamiruntu varuvatum, pōrp payiṟciyil talai ciṟantatu mākiya paṭai mūlappaṭai eṉappaṭṭatu. tirukkuṟaḷ itaṉait tol paṭai eṉak kūṟukiṉṟatu. aracaṉ ivarkaḷai eppoḻutum pōrukku āyattamāka vaittiruntāṉ. taṉakku utaviyākavuḷḷa naṭpu aracar utaviya paṭai naṭpup paṭai eṉappaṭṭatu. ippaṭaiyiṉar nampikkai uṭaiyavarkaḷāka iruppārkaḷō eṉpatil cantēkam iruntatu. ākavē ippaṭaiyiṉar muṉ eccarikkaiyōṭu payaṉpaṭuttappaṭṭārkaḷ. etirikaḷiṭamiruntu akappaṭuttappaṭṭārkaḷ allatu etiriyiṉ paṭaiyai viṭṭu vilaki vantavarkaḷ pakaippaṭaiyiṉar eṉappaṭ ṭārkaḷ. nāṭṭup paṭaiyōṭu ivarkaḷaic cērttup pōrukku aṉuppu vatil kavaṉam celuttappaṭṭatu. vēṭṭuvap paṭaiyiṉar pōril kiṭaikkum koḷḷaip poruḷkaḷukkākap pōr ceytaṉar. pōrk kālattil nāṭṭiliruntu tiraṭṭappaṭṭavarkaḷ aṭaṅkiya paṭai nāṭṭup paṭai eṉappaṭṭatu. kūliyiṉ poruṭṭup pōr ceyvōr kūlip paṭaiyiṉar eṉa aṟiyappaṭṭaṉar.
paṭai alaku patti eṉappaṭṭatu. iḵtu oru tēr, oru yāṉai, mūṉṟu kutirai, aintu kālāḷ koṇṭatu.
59. yāṉaip paṭai
yāṉaikaḷ pōrmuṉaiyil niṉṟu pōr ceyyumpaṭiyum, aṇiyai viṭṭu vilakik kuḻappam ceyyātirukkum paṭiyum payiṟṟap paṭṭaṉa. avaṟṟiṉ uṭal tōl pōrvaiyāl kākkappaṭṭatu. yāṉai kaḷai veppa kālattil payaṉpaṭuttāmal viṭuvatu virumpappaṭṭatu. avai etiriyiṉ paṭaiyait tākki aṇiyaik kulaittatu māttira mallāmal vēlikaḷaiyum, kūṭāraṅkaḷaiyum, araṇ ceyyappaṭṭa iṭaṅkaḷaiyum aḻittaṉa. pōr yāṉaikaḷiṉ kompukaḷil irumpi ṉāl ceyyappaṭṭa pūṇkaḷ iṟukkappaṭṭaṉa. pūṇkaḷ kimpuri eṉap paṭṭaṉa. cila camayaṅkaḷil kompukaḷil kūriya vāḷkaḷ kaṭṭappaṭṭaṉa. matil kataviṉ mītu pāyntu ataṉai uṭaittaṟkup pūṇkaḷ utaviyāka iruntaṉa. pākaṉait tavira iruvar allatu mūvar ataṉ mītiruntārkaḷ. ovvoru yāṉaiyum ciṟu kālāṭ paṭaiyāl pātukākkappaṭṭatu. pōr ceyyātavarkaḷ vaṇṭikaḷuṭaṉ piṉṉē ceṉṟārkaḷ. yāṉaikaḷ mika ariya uṭaimaikaḷākak karutappaṭṭaṉa. aracaṉuṭaiya veṟṟi yāṉaip paṭaiyiṉ tiṟamaiyaip poṟuttatāka iruntatu. kōpaṅ koṇṭa oru yāṉai āyiram kutiraikaḷukkuc camam eṉak karutap paṭṭatu. araca vakuppiṉar yāṉaiyaip payaṉpaṭuttiṉar. pōr toṭaṅ kuvataṟku muṉ yāṉaikku matu ūṭṭutalum vaḻakkāka iruntatu. yāṉai mītu koṭi nāṭṭappaṭṭiruntatu.
13ām nūṟṟāṇṭil intiyāvukku vanta cīṉap pirayāṇi oruvaṉ eḻutiyiruppatu varumāṟu:
“cōḻa aracaṉiṭattil aṟupatiṉāyiram pōr yāṉaikaḷ niṟkiṉṟaṉa. ovvoṉṟum ēḻu allatu eṭṭaṭi uyaramuṭaiyatu. pōr ceyyum pōtu yāṉaikaḷ mutukiṉ mēl vīṭu1kaḷaik koṇṭu celkiṉṟaṉa. avaṟṟuḷ pōr vīrar iruntu tolaivil niṟpavarkaḷ mītu ampu eytum, aṇmaiyil niṟpavarkaḷai īṭṭiyāl kuttiyum pōr ceyvar”.
60. kutiraip paṭai
kutiraikaḷ irumpuk kavacamiṭṭuk kākkappaṭṭaṉa. vīrar, vil, īṭṭi, vāḷ eṉpavaṟṟait tāṅkiyiruntaṉar. kutiraikaḷukkuk kaṭivāḷa miṭappaṭṭatu eṉṟum, cēṇam iṭappaṭavillai eṉṟum kirēkkar kūṟiyirukkiṉ ṟaṉar. vēvu pārppataṟkum etiriyiṉ paṭaiyai ūṭuruvic celvataṟkum kutiraip paṭai payaṉpaṭuttappaṭṭatu. kutiraip paṭaiyil kutiraikaḷaip paḻakkuvōrum vēlaikkārarum iruntaṉar. kauṭa liyar kutiraikaḷiṉ patiṉāṟu cāriyaikaḷaip paṟṟi kuṟippiṭṭuḷḷār. patiṉāṟu vakaik kaṭi vāḷaṅkaḷum āṟu vakai muṭkaḷum kuṟippiṭap paṭṭuḷḷaṉa. oṭṭakaṅkaḷ piṟkālaṅkaḷil payaṉpaṭuttappaṭṭaṉa.
61. tērp paṭai
tērkaḷil iraṇṭu kutiraikaḷ pūṭṭappaṭṭaṉa. avaṟṟil pōr ceypavaṉum tērppākaṉum niṟkak kūṭiyatāka iruntatu. pōr ceypavaṉ iṭappuṟattil niṉṟāṉ. tērkaḷiṉ vaṭivam ikkālam teṉṉintiya kōyilkaḷil kāṇappaṭum tērkaḷiṉ vaṭivai ottiruntatu. avai viraivil cellak kūṭiyaṉa. kaliṅkattup paraṇi mutaliya ilak kiyaṅkaḷiṟ kūṟappaṭuvaṉa koṇṭu itaṉai aṟiya muṭikiṟatu. tērkaḷ cama nilaṅkaḷil māttiram payaṉpaṭuttappaṭṭaṉa. tēril cāratiyait tavira iraṇṭu pōr ceyyum vīrar iruntaṉar eṉṟu mekastīṉas kūṟiyuḷḷaṉar. tērppākaṉ kavacamaṇintu kaiyil villaip piṭit tiruntāṉ. vaṭanāṭṭil tēr celuttuvōṉ cūtaṉ eṉa aṟiyap paṭṭāṉ. avaṉ pōrkkaḷattil kaṇṭa kāṭcikaḷaiyum, veṟṟi kaḷaiyum pāṭalkaḷākap pāṭiṉāṉ. avaṉ aracariṉ varalāṟ ṟāciriyaṉākavum perumai aṭaintāṉ.
62. kālāṭ paṭai
kālāṭ paṭaiyiṉar pavaṉi cellavum akaḻ veṭṭavum, matilkaḷ eḻuppavum, irākkālat tākkutalkaḷaic camāḷikkavum, ekkālattum evvakai iṭattum pōr ceyyavum āyattamāka irukkumpaṭi paḻakkappaṭṭiruntārkaḷ. kaṭṭāya vēlaikkākat tiraṭṭappaṭṭōr paṇṭaṅkaḷaiyum, pōrk karuvikaḷaiyum, kāyappaṭṭōraiyum eṭuttuc ceṉṟaṉar. 
63. pōrk kaṭṭaḷaikaḷ
pattu, nūṟu, āyiram eṉṉum kūṭṭaṅkaḷākap paṭai pirikkappaṭ ṭiruntatu. yāṉaikaḷ, kutiraikaḷ, tērkaḷukkup poṟuppāṉa ati kārikaḷ iruntārkaḷ. cēṉātipati paṭaikaḷiṉ talaivaṉāka iruntāṉ. ippeyar pattup pēraṭaṅkiya paṭaip piriviṉ talaivaṉaik kuṟippa tāvum iruntatu. makā cēṉātipati, nāyakaṉ eṉṉum talaivar muṭik kuriya irāca kumāraṉai otta uyarnta nilaiyiluḷḷavarkaḷāka iruntaṉar. aracaṉ peyaraḷavil ellārilum mēlāṉa taḷapatiyāka iruntāṉ.
kaṭṭaḷaikaḷ camikkaikaḷālum, vāttiyaṅkaḷai vēṟupaṭa olikkum olikaḷālum aṟivikkappaṭṭaṉa. eḻutappaṭṭa ōlaic curuḷai ampil kaṭṭi eytu ceytikaḷ aṟivikkappaṭṭaṉa. ovvoru ciṟiya irāṇuva alakukkum ataṉ koṭi iruntatu. mutaṉmaiyāṉa vīrar taṉittaṉi aṭaiyāḷamuḷḷa koṭiyai vaittiruntaṉar eṉṟu māpāratam kūṟukiṉṟatu. cakuṉaṅ kūṟuvōrum pulavarkaḷum etiriyait tākkuvataṟku ēṟṟa nērattaik kūṟiṉārkaḷ. appōtu avarkaḷ pōr vīrarukku uṟcākam ūṭṭiṉārkaḷ. pōr toṭaṅku muṉ paṭaikkumuṉ veḷiccam kāṭṭappaṭṭatu. paṭai, nāḷoṉṟukku iraṇṭu yōcaṉai tūram ceṉṟatu. yōcaṉai eṉpatu 32,000 muḻam koṇṭa tūram. caṅku, kompu mutaliya vāttiyaṅkaḷum palavakaip paṟaikaḷum pōril olikkappaṭṭaṉa.
64. aṇivakuppu
cātāraṇa aṇivakuppu camaviyūkam eṉappaṭṭatu. ataṟku matti, iru ciṟakukaḷ, iru ciṟakukaḷaiyum aṭutta iru pakkaṅkaḷ eṉa aintu pakutikaḷuṇṭu. ivaṟṟil mottam 45 tēr, 45 yāṉai, 225 kutirai, 675 kālāṭkaḷ uṇṭu. ivaṟṟōṭu kāvaṟ paṭai tuṇaip paṭai aṭaṅkiya 4,050 vīrarkaḷ koṇṭa cēṉaiyai oru paṭai eṉalām.
ovvoru varicaikkum iṭaiyil aintu muḻattūramum, oru vīraṉukkum maṟṟa vīraṉukkum iṭaiyil pattu aṅkula veḷiyumiruntaṉa. yāṉaikaḷ mattiyiṉ muṉ niṟuttappaṭṭaṉa. tērkaḷ iraṇṭu ciṟaku kaḷiṉ muṉ allatu piṉ niṉṟaṉa. tērkaḷillāviṭil kutiraip paṭai aṇiyiṉ pakkaṅkaḷaik kāttatu. yāṉaip paṭaiyiṉoru pakuti cēmap paṭaiyāka niṟuttappaṭṭiruntatu. kavacamaṇintavarkaḷ muṉṉaṇiyilum, maṟṟavarkaḷ pakka aṇikaḷilum, villāḷar iraṇṭām aṇiyilum niṉṟārkaḷ.
kampa aṇi etiriyai nēr varicaiyākat tākkuvatu. kaḻuku aṇi, kaḻuku pōl iraṇṭu pakka aṇikaḷuṭaṉ ceṉṟu tākkuvatu. ūci muṉai aṇi pakka aṇikaḷaiyum, vilā aṇikaḷaiyum uḷḷuk kiḻuttuk koṇṭu taṉṉilum atika eṇṇuḷḷa etiriyiṉ paṭaiyait tākkuvatu. pāmpu vaḷaivu aṇi, pāmpu pōla vaḷaintu ceṉṟu pakai varait tākkuvatu. vaṭṭa aṇi eṅkum paṭaimukam iruppatu pōlat tōṉṟumpaṭi vaṭṭamāka amaikkappaṭuvatu. ivvāṟu pala aṇi vakuppukkaḷiruntaṉa.
etiriyiṉ talaivarkaḷaik kolvataṟku vekumatikaḷ vaḻaṅkap paṭṭaṉa. aracaṉaik kolpavaṉukku 100,000 paṇamum, paṭaittalai vaṉaik kolpavaṉukku 50,000 paṇamum, yāṉaiyaik kolpavaṉukku 5,000 paṇamum, kutiraiyaik kolpavaṉukku 1000 paṇamum, ciṟu atikārikaḷaik kolpavaṉukku 100 paṇamum, kāvalarkaḷaik kol pavaṉukku 20 paṇamum vaḻaṅkappaṭṭaṉa. paṭaiyiṉ piṉ maruntu utavum paṭai iruntateṉṟum, paṇi ceyyum peṇkaḷ piṉṉē niṉṟu uṟcākam ūṭṭiṉārkaḷ eṉṟum kauṭaliyar kūṟiyuḷḷār. taṉippaṭṭa paṭai, paṭaikku vēṇṭiya poruḷai muṉṉamē koṇṭu ceṉṟu cērttatu.1
65. pōr āyutaṅkaḷ
palavakaip pērāyutaṅkaḷ iruntaṉa. muṉṉāl entirak karuvikaḷ ceṉṟaṉa. cakkaraṅkaḷ cuḻalumpōtu kavaṇil kaṟkaḷai eṟintaṉa. muḷ irumput taṇṭāyutaṅkaḷ (nūṟṟu varaikkolli) itikāca kālattil aṟiyappaṭṭiruntaṉa. kōṭṭai matilkaḷil kal eṟiyum entiraṅkaḷ nāṭṭap paṭṭiruntaṉa. neruppup paṭaikkalaṅkaḷ payaṉpaṭuttap paṭṭaṉa. neruppup paṭaik kalaṅkaḷ eṉpaṉa neruppaip koṇṭu cellum ampukaḷ. īṭṭikaḷil palavakaikaḷ iruntaṉa. potuvāṉa īṭṭi muṟṟilum ulōkattiṉāl ceyyappaṭṭiruntatu. ataṉ nīḷam aintaṭi eṭṭu aṅkulam. cila marakkaip piṭiyum ulōkamuṉaiyum uṭaiyavai. tōmaram eṉpatu yāṉaip paṭaiyiṉ mukkiya āyutam; atu nīṇṭa īṭṭi. tiricūlam, cakkaram, kavaṇ, taṇṭu, cammaṭṭi, mūṉṟu muṉaikaḷuṭaiya kaṇṭa kōṭāri mutaliya āyutaṅkaḷum payaṉpaṭuttap paṭṭaṉa. vaccirameṉpatu eṟipaṭai. vāḷkaḷil pala vakaikaḷ iruntaṉa. avai nīṇṭum oṭuṅkiyum iruntaṉa. kaippiṭikaḷ kompu, tantam, maram, mūṅkil eṉpavaikaḷāliṭappaṭṭaṉa. vil uyar vakuppiṉarāl payaṉ paṭuttappaṭṭatu. atu paṉai, pirampu, vayiramaram, kompu eṉpavaṟṟāl ceyyappaṭṭatu. nalla vil aintaṭi eṭṭu eṅkula nīḷamuṭaiyatu. nāṇ, caṇal, mūṅkil nār, vilaṅkukaḷiṉ narampukaḷāka iruntaṉa. ampai viṭumuṉ atu nāṇil vaittuk kātu varai iḻukkappaṭṭatu. cuyamvarattil ampeyvatu mutaliṭam peṟṟiruntatu. taṟkāppukkuriya karuvikaḷ pala payaṉpaṭuttappaṭṭaṉa. talai, tōḷ, uṭal, muḻaṅkāl kaḷaik kākkum kavacaṅkaḷ iruntaṉa.
66. kōṭṭaiyum pācaṟaiyum
kōṭṭaikaḷiṉ amaippu iṭaṅkaḷukkēṟpa vēṟupaṭṭiruntaṉa. kōṭṭaiyai akaḻ allatu malai araṇ ceytatu. ciṟpanūl pat toṉpatu vakaik kōṭṭaikaḷaip paṟṟik kuṟippiṭukiṉṟatu. kōṭṭai perumpālum nāṭṭiṉ ellaiyil kaṭṭappaṭṭiruntatu. ataṟku mūṉṟu akaḻkaḷiruntaṉa. avai muṟaiyē 56, 48, 40 muḻa akalamuṭai yavai. ovvoru akaḻikkumiṭaiyil nāṉku muḻa veḷiyiruntatu. akaḻkaḷiṉ āḻam akalattilum pāti aḷaviṉatāka iruntatu. uḷ akaḻiṉ piṉ 24 muḻam uyarnta mēṭai iruntatu. itupōl irumaṭi akalattil nañcu muḷ maraṅkaḷum ceṭikaḷum naṭappaṭṭiruntaṉa. ataṉ piṉ 24 muḻa uyaramum, 12 aṭi akalamuḷḷa matil kaṭṭappaṭṭiruntaṉa. kōpuraṅkaḷiṉiṭaiyē iraṇṭu māṭikaḷuṭaiya kaṭṭiṭaṅkaḷ iruntaṉa. avaṟṟiṉ mēl māṭiyil mūṉṟu villāṭkaḷ maṟaintu niṟkak kūṭiyatāka iruntatu. matilaic cuṟṟi uṭpuṟattil vīti ceṉṟatu. pakaivar muṟṟukai iṭuṅkālaṅkaḷil caṭutiyil ceṉṟu avarait tākkutaṟku veḷiyē cellum iṭaṅkaḷ iruntaṉa. kōṭṭai vāyiṟkatavukaḷ pala maraṅkaḷai oṉṟiṉ mītu oṉṟāka vaittup poruttic ceyyappaṭ ṭiruntaṉa. avai iraṇṭu ciṟakukaḷāka amaikkap paṭṭiruntaṉa. avai irumpuc calākaikaḷāl tāḻiṭappaṭṭaṉa. kōṭṭaiyuḷ curuṅkai vaḻikaḷiruntaṉa.
pācaṟai eṉpatu paṭaṅkukaḷāliṭappaṭṭa araṇ ceyyappaṭṭa kūṭāram. itu cōtiṭariṉ ālōcaṉaiyōṭu ciṟpikaḷāl karuttōṭu vakukkappaṭṭatu. iḵtu iṭaṅkaḷukkēṟpa vaṭṭamāka, nīṇṭa caturamāka allatu caturamāka amaikkappaṭṭatu. itaṟku nāṉku vāyilkaḷum piṉṉē ilēcāṉa araṇkaḷumiruntaṉa. iḵtu āṟu pirivukaḷākap pirikkappaṭṭiruntatu. aracaṉuṟaiyumiṭam mutaliraṇṭu aṟaikaḷāka iruntatu. atikārikaḷ teṟkil iruntārkaḷ. yāṉaikaḷum kutirai kaḷum kaṭṭumiṭam vaṭakkiliruntatu. atu oru ciṟiya paṭṭiṉamāka iruntatu. vāttiyakkārarum, vēṭṭuvarum kūṭārattukku veḷiyil taṅkiṉārkaḷ.
67. nampikkaikaḷ
cōtiṭattilum cakuṉattilum nampikkai iruntatu. eri koḷḷi viḻuvatu nāṭṭiluḷḷa periyavariṉ maraṇattukku aṟikuṟi eṉak karutap paṭṭatu. kūntal virittirukkum peṇṇaip pārttal tītu eṉak karutap paṭṭatu. ciṟuvarait tīmaikaḷiliruntu kāppataṟkāka aimpaṭaittāli kaṭṭappaṭṭatu. pēykaḷai ōṭṭutaṟku veṇkaṭuku pukaikkappaṭṭatu. ālamarattilum vēṟu cila maraṅkaḷilum pēyuṟaivatākak karutappaṭṭatu. pāmpu cantira cūriyarai viḻuṅkuvatāl kirakaṇa muṇṭākiṟateṉak karutappaṭṭatu. kākam karaivatu viruntiṉar varuvataṟku aṟikuṟi eṉa nampappaṭṭatu. tolaiviṭattiluḷḷa oruvar oruvarai niṉaippatāl tummaluṇṭākiṟateṉak karutappaṭṭatu. nākattiṉ talaiyil irattiṉam irukkiṟateṉa nampappaṭṭatu. palli colvatu naṟcakuṉa mākavō tīya cakuṉamākavō koḷḷappaṭṭatu. uṉṉamaram (ilavu) vāṭuvatu tīya cakuṉamākak karutappaṭṭatu. pōrkkaḷattil pēy tiriva tākavum, pēykaḷ piṇam tiṉpatākavum nampikkai iruntatu. vēppilai ciṟuvaraip pēykaḷiliruntu kākkum eṉa nampappaṭṭatu. pōril iṟantavar vīra corkkamaṭaivar eṉṉum nampikkai iruntatu. valak kaṇ tuṭippatu naṟcakuṉamākavum. iṭakkaṇ tuṭippatu tīya cakuṉamākavum koḷḷappaṭṭaṉa. ciṟuvarukkuk kaṇṇūṟu paṭāmal avar talai mayiril neyyum veṇ ciṟu kaṭukum pūcappaṭṭaṉa. 
68. pōkkuvarattu
perumpālum makkaḷ kāl naṭaiyākap pōkkuvarattuc cey tārkaḷ. palavakai vaṇṭikaḷ, pallakku, tēr, kaḻutai, erutu, yāṉai mutaliyaṉavum muṟkālap pōkkuvarattuc cātaṉaṅkaḷāka iruntaṉa. ūrti, oḻukai, cakaṭu, cākāṭu, vaiyam mutaliyaṉa vaṇṭiyaik kuṟikkum peyarkaḷ. vaṇṭikaḷum kaḻutaikaḷum potimāṭukaḷum paṇṭaṅkaḷai ōriṭattiliruntu ōriṭattukku eṭuttuccellap payaṉpaṭuttappaṭṭaṉa. aracarum perumakkaḷum tēr, yāṉai, pallakku mutaliyavaikaḷil ceṉṟārkaḷ. nīril celvōr ōṭaṅkaḷil ceṉṟaṉar. ōṭaṅkaḷil pala vakaikaḷ iruntaṉa. ōṭam, ampi, tōṇi, teppam, paṭaku, kalam, paḵṟi, catā, pōtam, toḷḷam, pakaṭu, paṭṭikai, pāṭṭimār, paṭuvai, puṇai, mitavai, vaḷḷam, timil mutaliyaṉa ōṭaṅkaḷaik kuṟikkum peyarkaḷ. ivai vevvēṟu vakai ōṭaṅkaḷaik kuṟippaṉavākalām. marakkalaṅ kaḷiṉ muṉpuṟam yāṉai mukam, kutirai mukam, arimukam pōṉṟu ceyyappaṭṭiruntatu. marakkalaṅkaḷukkup pāy maraṅkaḷum paṭaṅkum (pāyum) iruntaṉa.
69. ōviyam
mika muṟkālam mutal ōviyak kalaiyil tiṟamai peṟṟu viḷaṅ kiṉārkaḷ. muṟkāla eḻuttu muṟai ōviya vaṭivilēyē amaintiruntatu. kaṟkāla vāḻkkaiyilirunta makkaḷ kukaic cuvarkaḷil tīṭṭiya ōviyaṅkaḷ kaṇṭupiṭikkappaṭṭuḷḷaṉa. avai tiṟamaiyāka eḻutappaṭṭuḷḷaṉa. mokañcatārō makkaḷiṉ muttiraikaḷil aḻakiya ōviyaṅkaḷ veṭṭappaṭṭuḷḷaṉa. avai ikkālam varaiyappaṭum ciṟanta ōviyaṅ kaḷōṭu otta kalaittiṟamai uṭaiyaṉavāka irukkiṉṟaṉa. acantāk kukai ōviyaṅkaḷ ulakap pukaḻ peṟṟavai. caṅkakāla nūlkaḷil ōviyak kalaiyaip paṟṟiya kuṟippukaḷ kāṇappaṭukiṉṟaṉa. araṇmaṉaic cuvar kaḷilum, kōyil cuvarkaḷilum, celvariṉ māḷikaic cuvarkaḷilum aḻakiya ōviyaṅkaḷ varaiyappaṭṭiruntaṉa. akkālak kōyilkaḷil eḻuttu nilai maṇṭapam eṉa oru pakuti iruntatu. aṅku perumpālum purāṇa campantamāṉa ōviyaṅkaḷ varaiyappaṭṭiruntaṉa.
itaṉai,
“intiraṉ pūcai yivaḷakalikai yivaḷ
ceṉṟa kavutamaṉ ciṉaṉuṟak kalluru
voṉṟiya paṭiyiteṉ ṟuraicey vōru
miṉṉam palapala veḻuttu nilaimaṇṭapam”
eṉap paripāṭal aṭikaḷ kuṟippiṭukiṉṟaṉa.
“cuṭuma ṇōṅkiya neṭunilai maṉaitoṟu
maiyaṟu paṭivattu vāṉavar muṉivar
evvakai yuyirkaḷu vuvamaṅ kāṭṭi
kaṇkala rōviyaṅ kaṇṭu niṟkunarum”
eṉṉum maṇimēkalai aṭikaḷ akkāla maṉaikaḷil ōviyaṅkaḷ eḻutappaṭṭiruntamaiyai naṉku viḷakkukiṉṟaṉa. paḻantamiḻ ilakkiyaṅ kaḷil maṭalēṟutal eṉṉum oru vaḻakkam kūṟappaṭukiṉṟatu. oruvaṉ tāṉ kātalitta peṇṇaip peṟamuṭiyāta pōtu avaṉ avaḷaip pōṉṟa paṭamoṉṟai eḻuti, uyarttik koṇṭu paṉai maṭṭaiyāl ceyta kutiraiyilēṟi vītiyil varuvāṉ. itaṉāl avaṉ kātalikkum peṇ yāreṉa aṟiyak kūṭiyatāka iruntatu. itaṉāl potumakkaḷum ōviyam varaiyum tiṟamai peṟṟiruntārkaḷ eṉat terikiṟatu.
70. ciṟpam
ciṟpak kalai intiyāvil mikap paḻaiya kālattil vaḷarcci yaṭaintiruntatu. mokañcatārōvil pala aḻakiya cuṭumaṇ pāvai kaḷum, kallil cetukkappaṭṭa maṉita uruvaṅkaḷum, ulōkattil vārkkappaṭṭa nāṭṭiyap peṇṇiṉ uruvamum kaṇṭupiṭikkap paṭṭaṉa. kallil cetukkappaṭṭa cilai oṉṟu kaikaḷum talaiyum illāmal kāṇappaṭṭatu. itu kirēkka ciṟpak kalaiyai otta kalait tiṟamai peṟṟatāka aṟiñar pukaḻntuḷḷārkaḷ. ulōkattil vārkkap paṭṭa naṭaṉamātu uruvattaip palar pukaḻntu eḻutiyuḷḷārkaḷ. ēṟattāḻa ki.mu. 3000-il intiya makkaḷ ciṟpak kalaiyil mika muṉṉēṟ ṟam peṟṟiruntārkaḷ. tamiḻar peṟṟirunta tiṟamaiyaik kuṟittuc caṅka ilakkiyaṅkaḷil kāṇkiṉṟōm.
“kallu mulōkamum ceṅkalu maramum
maṇṇuñ cutaiyun tantamum vaṇṇamum
kaṇṭacark karaiyu meḻuku meṉṟivai
pattē ciṟpat toḻiṟkuṟup pāvaṉa”
eṉat tivākaram kūṟukiṉṟatu.
teṉṉintiyak kōyilkaḷil karuvaṟaiyilirukkum tiruvuruvaṅ kaḷ kallil cetukkappaṭṭu vantaṉa. piṟkālattil cempum piṟa ulō kaṅkaḷum cērttu urukki vārkkappaṭṭaṉa. ulōkattil vārkkap paṭṭa uruvaṅkaḷ tiruviḻāk kālaṅkaḷil veḷiyē koṇṭu cellap paṭṭaṉa. ivvakai uruvaṅkaḷum naṭarācat tiruvuruvamum ulaka makkaḷiṉ pārāṭṭaip peṟṟuḷḷatu. iṉṟu teṉṉintiyā ilaṅkai mutaliya nāṭukaḷil nūtaṉa poruṭkāṭci cālaikaḷil vaikkappaṭ ṭirukkum paḻaṅkālac ciṟpaṅkaḷ campantappaṭṭa poruḷkaḷ tamiḻariṉ ciṟpat tiṟamaiyai veḷiyiṭukiṉṟaṉa. cōḻar, pallavar kālaṅkaḷil eṭukkappaṭṭa kaṟkōyilkaḷum, malaikkuṭaivuk kōyilkaḷum kaṟ kaḷil cetukkappaṭṭirukkum vilaṅku, maṉitar, paṟavaikaḷ, marañ ceṭikaḷiṉ vaṭivaṅkaḷum tamiḻariṉ ciṟpat tiṟaṉai eṉṟum kāṭṭik koṇṭirukkum aḻiyāc ciṉṉaṅkaḷākum
71. maruntu
maruttuvakkalai nōykaḷait tīrkkum mūlikaikaḷaik kaṇṭu piṭippatiliruntu toṭaṅkukiṟatu. mūlikaikaḷiṉ kuṇaṅkaḷ naṉku aṟiyappaṭṭiruntaṉa. vātamaṭakki, vaṇṭu kolli, kirantināyaṉ, poṉṉāṅkaṇṇi pōṉṟu avvam mūlikaikaḷukkuḷḷa kuṇaṅkaḷē avaṟṟukkup peyarkaḷāka vaḻaṅkiṉa. mūlikai akarātikaḷil mikap pala mūlikaikaḷiṉ peyarkaḷ kāṇappaṭukiṉṟaṉa. patārttakuṇa cintāmaṇi eṉṉum nūl piṟkālattiṟ ceyyappaṭṭatāyiṉum, atu makkaḷ mūlikaikaḷaip paṟṟi muṉṉamē aṟintiruntavaṟṟait taḻuvic ceyyap paṭṭa nūlākum. kiyāḻam, kuḷikai, cūraṇam, ilēkiyam, tailam, centūram eṉṉum pala vakaikaḷil maruntākap payaṉpaṭuttappaṭ ṭuḷḷatu. acōkac cakkaravartti vilaṅkukaḷukkum makkaḷukkum maruttuva nilaiyaṅkaḷai niṟuviṉār eṉac carittiram kūṟukiṉṟatu. ivvakai nilaiyaṅkaḷ ilaṅkaiyilum niṟuvappaṭṭiruntaṉaveṉṟu makāvamicam kūṟukiṉṟatu. acōkar kālattukkup pala nūṟṟāṇṭukaḷiṉ muṉ maruttuvakkalai intiyāvil vaḷarcciyaṭaintiruntatu. alekcāntar intiyāviliruntu pāmpukkaṭi vaittiyarkaḷaik kirēkka nāṭṭukkuk koṇṭu ceṉṟār eṉak kirēkka āciriyarkaḷ kūṟiyirukkiṉṟaṉar. kippakiriṭṭas eṉṉum kirēkkar intiyariṉ maruttuva muṟaikaḷaik kaṟṟu avaṟṟaik kaiyāṇṭār eṉac collappaṭuvatuṇṭu.
tamiḻar kaiyāṇṭa vaittiya muṟai piṟkālattil citta muṟai eṉa vaḻaṅkukiṟatu. irācayaṉa muṟaiyāṉa tamiḻariṉ maruttuvakkalai paḻaimaiyāṉatum, payaṉaḷikkak kūṭiyatum, tamiḻnāṭṭiṉ poruḷā tāra nilai, kāla nilaikaḷukku ēṟṟatumākum. atu citta vaittiyam eṉappaṭum. ataṉ nōkkam, taṭuppu, kuṇappaṭuttuvatu, iḻantu pōṉa valimaiyait tirumpap peṟuvatu eṉṉum mūṉṟu kūṟukaḷai uṭaiyatu. tiṭamāṉa uṭalil tiṭamāṉa maṉam eṉṉum koḷkai uṟutippaṭ ṭiruntatu. uṭal illāviṭil oru pēṟum kiṭṭātu; uṭalillā viṭṭāl vīṭu kiṭṭātu eṉac cittar kūṟiṉar.
“tēkamirutā lallō tittellā māṭalām
tēkamirun tākkāṟ cēralām pūraṇam
tēkamirun tākkāṟ ceyalellām pārkkalām
tēkamirun tākkāṟ cēralām muttiyē” (tirumūlar karukkiṭai vaittiyam)
ātiyilē cittaṉārākiya civaṉār ceyta maruttuva nūl ēḻu laṭcam pāṭalkaḷuṭaiyatu. piṉ nanti, caṉakar, caṉātar, caṉāntaṉar, caṉaṟkumārar, tirumūlar, patañcali, akattiyar, pulattiyar, pucuṇṭar, karuvūrar, taṉvantiri, caṭṭaimuṉi, tēraiyar, yūkimuṉi mutaliya palar nūl ceytaṉar. ivai maṇi (iracamaṇi), mantiram, maruntu mutaliya vaṟṟaik kūṟukiṉṟaṉa. mūlikai, uppu, tīnīr1, upavācam, 2uṭaṟporuḷ, pāṭāṇam, ulōkam, cattu3, iracakkuḷikai, yōkam eṉṉum pattuc cikiccai muṟaikaḷait tirumūlar kūṟiyirukkiṉṟār. mantirameṉpatu yōkattilum maṇi eṉpatu iracak kuḷikaikaḷilum aṭaṅkum. mūlikaikaḷ cūraṇam, iḻakiyam (ilēkiyam), meḻuku eṉpaṉa. ivai makkaḷuṟai eṉappaṭum. kaṭṭikaḷukku maruntākum tailam, cārāyattil ūṟa viṭappaṭṭa maruntukaḷ aṟuvai campantamāṉavai; centūram, cuṇṇam, ceynīr, tīnīr, cattu, maṇi mutaliyaṉa, paspam (cāmpal) eṉpatil aṭaṅkum. immuṟai citta maruttuvattil māttiramuṇṭu.
oppuṟai (ōmiyōpati pōṉṟatu), etiruṟai (alōpati), kalap puṟai eṉa mūṉṟu vakai maruntu muṟaikaḷ uṇṭu. uppu vakaikaḷ 25, pāṭāṇam 64, ulōkam 9, ulōkac cattukaḷ 120, maruntu mūlikaikaḷ 1008. nāṭi pārttu vaittiyam ceytal cittamuṟai. iṭakalai, piṅkalai, cuḻi muṉai eṉa nāṭi mūṉṟu. maruttuvaṉ nāṭiyaip pārttu vātam, pittam, cilēṭṭumam eṉṉum mūṉṟum iyalpāy irukkiṉṟaṉavā allatu iyalpukku māṟāka irukkiṉṟaṉavā eṉa aṟikiṟāṉ. aṭutta paṭiyil kaṇ, nākku, uṭal, malam, mūttiram, cattam mutaliyavaṟṟaip pārttalōṭu uṭalait toṭṭup pārttum aṟiyappaṭum. citta vaittiyattaip piṉpaṟṟum tiruvaḷḷuvar, nōyaik kaṇṭupiṭi, ataṟkuk kāraṇattai aṟi, ataṟku maruntai ārāyntu pār, kāla nilaiyaik kavaṉi, mikap payaṉaḷippavaṟṟaic cey eṉak kūṟukiṉṟār. maruntuk kalai, nōyāḷi, maruttuvaṉ, maruntukaḷai araittō iṭittō piḻintō kalantu ceypavaṉ eṉṉum nāṉku pakutikaḷai uṭaiyatu. maruttuvacālai niṟuvuvatu muppattiraṇṭu aṟaṅkaḷuḷ oṉṟākac collappaṭṭuḷḷatu. āṉma caktiyiṉāl allatu maṉōcaktiyiṉāl māṟṟuvatu iṉṉoru muṟai. itu camayakuravarkaḷ muṉivarkaḷāl kaiyāḷappaṭṭa muṟai. pārvai pārttal, nīrōtik koṭuttal, mantiram cepittal pōṉṟavai āṉma cattiyāl nōyai āṟṟum muṟaiyil aṭaṅkum.
cārakam, cucurarutam, taṉvantiri nikaṇṭu eṉpaṉa vaṭa nāṭṭāriṉ maruttuva nūlkaḷ. ivaṟṟil muṉ kūṟappaṭṭa mūṉṟu uṟaikaḷaiyum kāṇa muṭiyātu. āyurvētam eṉpatu citta vaittiyamākum. āyurvētam eṉṉum peyaruṭaiya nūl āriya moḻiyil illai. taṉvantiri ki.pi. 500il vikkiramātittaṉiṉ araca capaiyiliruntavar. cucurutar avar kālattavar. cārakar avarukku muṉ viḷaṅkiyavar. aṭṭāṅka irutayam vākpātarāl 9ām nūṟṟāṇṭil ceyyappaṭṭatu. piṟkāla maruttuva nūlār cittar nūlkaḷaip payiṉṟum paspam, nāṭi, puṭam pōṭutal mutaliya muṟaikaḷai moḻi peyarttut tamatu nūlil cērttaṉar. cāraṅkatarariṉ caṅkitai 13ām nūṟṟāṇṭil ceyyappaṭṭatu. innūl, atu citta vaittiyattukkuk kaṭamaippaṭṭiruppataik kūṟukiṉṟatu. ceṉṉaiyil paṇṭitar kōpālāccāriyariṉ talaimaiyil kūṭiya āyurvēta mānāṭṭil avarum itu pōṉṟa karuttait terivikkiṉ ṟār. kaṇṇāl pārttal, toṭṭup pārttal, cattattaik kēṭṭup pārttal eṉṉum mūṉṟu cōtaṉaikaḷaic ceyvatē vaṭanāṭṭu muṟai. atarvaṇa vētattait tokuttu muṭittapiṉ āyur, artta, taṉur, kāntarva vētaṅkaḷai eḻutuvataṟkum tiṭṭamiṭappaṭṭatu. āyur vētameṉṉum nūl orupōtum eḻutappaṭavillai.
tamiḻaracariṉ viḻukaikkup piṉ citta vaittiyam vīḻcci yaṭaintatu (tamiḻ intiyā - mu.ci.pū.).
72. irēkai nūl
akattiyariṉ irēkai nūl cāmuttirikam eṉappaṭum. innūliṉ muḻup peyarum puruṭa cāmuttirika ilaṭcaṇam. itu cuppiramaṇiyak kaṭavuḷ akattiyarukkuk kūṟiyatākac collappaṭukiṟatu. itu uḷḷaṅ kai maṇikkaṭṭukaḷiluḷḷa irēkaikaḷ, varaikaḷ, maccam, āḷiṉ uyaram, neṭuppam, kaikaḷ, kālkaḷiṉ nīḷaṅkaḷaip pārttu maṉitariṉ kuṇā kuṇaṅkaḷai aṟiyumpaṭiyāṉa vitikaḷaik kūṟukiṉṟatu. oruvaṉatu uḷḷaṅkai civappēṟiyum, ciṟitākavum iruntāl avaṉukkuc celvamum nīṇṭa āyuḷum uṇṭu; taṭippāka iruntāl avaṉ kavalai uṭaiyavaṉāvāṉ. caṅkaip pōlum, cakkarattaip pōlum irēkaikaḷ iruntāl avaṉ atika varuvāy uṭaiyavaṉāyum, tarumam ceypavaṉāyum, taṉṉai aṭaintavarkaḷiṭattil tayāḷam uṭaiyava ṉākavum irup pāṉ. oruvaṉuṭaiya kaiyil macca irēkai allatu mīṉ pōṉṟa aṭaiyāḷam iruntāl avaṉ tayāḷamuṭaiyavaṉāka iruppāṉ. mūccukkuḻāy pōṉṟa irēkai iruntāl pukaḻ aṭai vāṉ. arivāḷ pōṉṟa irēkai iruntāl avaṉ tairiyamum ūkkamum uṭaiyava ṉāvāṉ. cāṭipōla iruntāl cāntamāṉavaṉāka iruppāṉ. cantiraṉaip pōla iruntāl kalvimāṉāvāṉ. ivvāṟu annūl pala ceytikaḷaik kūṟukiṉṟatu. ikkalai pāṇṭi nāṭṭi liruntu arēpiyāvukkuc ceṉṟu aṅku niṉṟum airōppāvukkuc ceṉṟatu. (mu.ci.pū.)
73. vāṉārāycci
tamiḻar periya kaṭal payaṇakkārarāka iruntaṉar. avarkaḷ tamatu payaṇaṅkaḷil irākkālattil cantiraṉum naṭcattiraṅkaḷum niṟkum iṭaṅkaḷaip pārppatu avarkaḷukku utaviyāka iruntatu. avarkaḷ mātam tētikaḷaik kāṭṭum kuṟippukaḷai eḻuti vaittapōtu cūriyaṉum cantiraṉum periyaṉavākat tōṉṟumpaṭi kuṟippiṭappaṭṭa ṉar. veḷiccamāṉa kirakaṅkaḷ oṉṟukkoṉṟu evvaḷavu tūrattil niṟkiṉṟaṉaveṉpatum kuṟippiṭappaṭṭatu. mātattukkut tiṅkaḷ eṉap peyariṭappaṭṭatum 28 naṭcattirak kūṭṭaṅkaḷ koḷḷappaṭuvatum tamiḻariṉ mātam tētik kaṇakku cantiramāṉa aḷavaiyāka iruntateṉat terivikkiṟatu. paḻaiya vaṭanāṭṭu ilakkiyaṅkaḷil nāṭkaḷai vāramākak koṇṭu kuṟippiṭum muṟai kāṇappaṭavillai. vāramuṟai yāṉa kaṇita muṟai tamiḻaruṭaiyatu. tamiḻar mēṟku nōkkic ceṉṟa pōtu yūpriṭṭicu taikirīcu āṟṟōraṅkaḷil kuṭiyēṟiṉārkaḷ. ākavē vāra muṟaiyāṉa kaṇita muṟaiyai ivarkaḷ annāṭṭil parappi ṉārkaḷ.
kirakaṅkaḷum naṭcattirak kūṭṭaṅkaḷum maṉitaṉuṭaiya palāpalaṉ kaḷil āṭci celuttukiṉṟaṉa eṉpatu mikap paḻaṅkālattil aṟiyap paṭṭiruntatu. cūriyaṉuṭaiya celvākku iyaṟkaip poruḷkaḷilum cantiraṉuṭaiya celvākku kaṭalvaṟṟup perukkukaḷilum iruntu varuvatai viññāṉikaḷ kūṟukiṉṟaṉar. ivvaṭippaṭaiyil varalāṟ ṟukku muṉ cōtiṭak kalai toṭaṅkiṟṟu. erikoḷḷi erintu viḻuvatu varavirukkum tīmaiyaik kāṭṭuvatākavum, cantira, cūriya kirakaṇaṅkaḷ keṭutalāṉavai eṉṟum karutappaṭṭaṉa. karuppamāṉa peṇ evaḷāvatu kirakaṇattaip pārkkamāṭṭāḷ.
paḻantamiḻar paruva kālattaik kār, kūtir, muṉpaṉi, piṉpaṉi, iḷa vēṉil, mutuvēṉil eṉa āṟu pirivukaḷākap pirittiruntārkaḷ. cūriyaṉ ciṅka rāciyil cellum kālam āvaṇiyāka iruntatu. muṟ kālattil āvaṇi āṇṭu toṭaṅkum mātamākavum, āṭi āṇṭiṉ iṟuti mātamākavum iruntaṉa. āvaṇi mātattil cūriyaṉai mukilkaḷ maṟaippatāl mantāramuṇṭākat toṭaṅkukiṟatu. kuḷir kālam kaḻintu veyil kāyat toṭaṅkum kālamākiya tait toṭakkattil tamiḻar poṅkal viḻāvaik koṇṭāṭiṉārkaḷ.
caṅka ilakkiyaṅkaḷil kaṇikaḷ eṉpōrāl kaliyāṇaṅkaḷukku nāḷ kuṟittal kuṟippiṭappaṭṭuḷḷatu. “mūvakaik kālamum neṟiyilāṟṟu vatāvatu pakalumiravum iṭaiviṭāmal ākāyattaip pārttu āṇṭu nikaḻum villum, miṉṉum, ūrkkōḷum, tūmamum, miṉ vīḻvum, kōḷ nilaiyum, maḻai nilaiyum piṟavum pārttuk kūṟutal” eṉa ivarkaḷaik kuṟittu iḷampūraṇar kūṟiyuḷḷār. kaṭṭilukku mēlē yuḷḷa mēṟkaṭṭiyil paṉṉiraṇṭu irācikaḷum eḻutappaṭṭiruntaṉa veṉṟu neṭunalvāṭai kūṟukiṟatu. kuṟiñci nila makkaḷ cantiraṉ parivaṭṭaṅkoḷḷum kālattil maṇam ceyvārkaḷ. paripāṭal, cilappatikāram, pattuppāṭṭu mutaliya nūlkaḷil āṅkāṅku vāṉa nūṟ kuṟippukaḷ kāṇappaṭukiṉṟaṉa.
74. celvaṉ vāḻum māḷikai
1celvaṉ vāḻum māḷikai iraṇṭākap pirikkappaṭṭiruntatu. muṉ puṟattil āṭavarum piṉpaṟattil makaḷirum vāḻntaṉar. vīṭṭut talaivaṉ taṉatu karumaṅkaḷaik kavaṉittuk koṇṭu mīḷvōrai upacarittāṉ. vīṭṭil ovvoru tēvaikkum vēṇṭiya pala aṟaika ḷiruntaṉa. vīṭṭai aṭuttu vicālamāṉa tōṭṭamiruntatu. tōṭṭat til pūñceṭikaḷum paḻamaraṅkaḷum uṇavukku vēṇṭiya kāy piñcukaḷ koṭukkum ceṭi koṭikaḷum uṇṭākkappaṭṭiruntaṉa. ataṉ mattiyil kiṇaṟiruntatu. tōṭṭam vīṭṭiṉ piṉ puṟattil iruntamai yiṉ vīṭṭiṉ talaiviyē ataṉaik kavaṉittāḷ. pūntōṭṭattil naṟumaṇa malarkaḷaip pūkkum mallikai mullai mutaliya koṭikaḷ paṭarntiruntaṉa. avaikaḷiṉiṭaiyē amaikkappaṭṭirunta mēṭai mītiruntu avaḷ ullācamākap poḻutu pōkkiṉāḷ. vīṭu mikac cuttamāka iruntatu. vīṭṭil teyvaṅkaḷ vaittu vaḻipaṭappaṭṭaṉa. kaṇavaṉum maṉaiviyum nilā muṟṟattil iruntu veṇ matiyaiyum viṇmīṉkaḷaiyum nōkki makiḻntārkaḷ. vīṭṭuc cuvarkaḷ āḷiṉuru vam piratipalikkumpaṭi miṉukkañ ceyyappaṭṭiruntaṉa. vīṭṭuk kūrai kaḷai aḻakiya tūṇkaḷ tāṅki niṉṟaṉa. tōṭṭattil nīrāl cūḻap paṭṭa nīrāḻi maṇṭapam iruntatu. atu kōṭaikālattil uṟaivataṟku ēṟṟatu. peṇkaḷ taṅkum pakutiyiṉ nāṟpuṟaṅkaḷilum aṟaikaḷ iruntaṉa. 
talaivaṉ uṟaiyum aṟaiyil pañcu mettaikaḷ iṭappaṭṭa iraṇṭu kaṭṭilkaḷ iruntaṉa. mettaiyiṉ nāṟpakkaṅkaḷilum aṇaikaḷ iṭappaṭṭiruntaṉa. talaip pakkattukku aṇmaiyil ularnta marattaṭṭu iruntatu. kālaiyil alaṅkarittuk koḷvataṟku vēṇṭiya cantaṉam, vācaṉait tailam, pūmālai mutaliyaṉa ataṉmītu vaikkappaṭṭiruntaṉa. taraiyil eccil umiḻum kāḷāñci iruntatu. aṟaikku veḷiyē vaḷarkkum kiḷikaḷ kūṭukaḷil iruntaṉa.
talaivaṉ kālaiyil eḻuntu kālaik kaṭaṉkaḷai muṭittapiṉ taṉṉai alaṅkarittāṉ. alaṅkārap poruḷkaḷil ciṟantavai cantaṉam, vācaṉait tiraviyaṅkaḷ eṉpaṉa. avaṉ vācaṉaip pukai ūṭṭappaṭṭa āṭaiyai uṭuttup pūmālaiyai aṇintāṉ. kaṇṇukku mai tīṭṭiṉāṉ; tāmpūlamiṭṭuc civanta itaḻkaḷukku arakkuk kūṭṭic ceyta cāyam pūciṉāṉ. talaiyai vāriṉāṉ. viralkaḷukku mōtiraṅ kaḷai aṇintāṉ. mēlē uttarikam tarittāṉ.

1. The progress of research into various phases of Indian antiquities is helping to pile up evidences to demonstrate the fact that the texure of Indian culture is
made of the work of non-Aryan and pre-Aryan threads crossed with the woof of Aryan Hinduistic character. In the light of these evidences the conviction has been gaining ground that the great process popularly known as Hinduism is nothing but a synthesis and harmonization of complex elements of Aryan, pre-Aryan, non-Aryan and aboriginal culture, a good deal of which must have been autocthonus and indigenous, that is to say, was born on, or sprung from the soil of Indian continent. It has become impossible to contradict the fact that aboriginal and Indian Aryan cultures have greatly contributed to the development of what has become to be known during historical times as characteristically Indian civilization. Sometimes the elements and types of aboriginal culture has been transformed and modified so as to fit into the ideals and systems of Aryan thought and culture. On the grounds indicated above, we may infer the, Upanishadic speculations originated wholly outside the pale of Vedic Brahmanism and had their source in the religio-philosophical thought currents already prevalent in India since pre-Aryan days. That a rich culture which had been flourishing in India for at least two millena before the advent of the Vedic Aryans, should produce philosophical thinking and religious ideas of refined types is no difficult to make, for, it is but normal to expect this evolution ... the pre-Vedic elements constituted the texure while the Vedic did probably no more than imprint the stamp. It would be historically more correct, therefore, to regard Upanishadic as much as Jaina and Buddhist thoughts as having their roots more in non-Vedic than in Vedic ideas. We also find the basic ideas of the Samkhya and Yoga permeate Jaina, Buddhist as well as the Upanishadic outlook and it is probable that the primitive Samkhya consisted the philosophical background par excellence of pre-Vedic Indian thought and Yoga consisted an essential element in the cultivation of matters concerning the spirit. Both Samkhya and Yoga had developed probably already in pre-Aryan India ... the origin of Upanishads was not at all Vedic. We must not forget the priestly classes and philosophical thinkers with their religious practices and ideas who existed in India from before the coming of the Indian Aryans. By Buddhas time they have probably been absorbed in the part of the Vedic society and came to called Brahmans - Back ground of Buddhist philosophy - Prof. Dr.B.B.Bhattacharia, M.A.D., Ph.D. Indo Asian Culture, No.1.

Long expected evidence is now appearing that they - Dravid Pandits - composed some Upanishads and Brahmanas and why not Vedas, engrafting there in the hymns, prayers and faith of illiterate Aryans? All these scriptures are inferior and easy compositions to philosophical works which issued from the schools of - Kapila before Buddah’s day there was or any Aryan settlement in the middle Ganges. The most important of these dark skinned tribes were Yadus and Turvasas. Even the Rishis or the chief priests of the Indo-Aryan tribes had to admit into their order the priests of these dark-skinned Aryans. The Vedic literature contains descriptions of white skinned and golden haired Rishis and dark skinned Rishis. After this admixure the Indo-Aryans became powerful enough to push on towards the east and south. They conquered the Dravidian kingdoms of the united provinces and northern Rajaputana, but did not succeed in penetrating further South or East. The Dravidian remained independent in Bihar, Bengal, Orissa, and Central Provinces, Gujarat, and Sindh; while the country to the south of Vindhya remained entirely uneffected by the invasion of the Indo-Aryans-Junior History of India - R.D.Banerji, M.A.
The non-Aryan magicians and Dravidians became Brahmans. South Indian tradition records numerous instances of Brahmans as taking wives from the lower castes. In many cases non-Brahmans were admitted into the Brahman castes as sufficient Brahmans were not available when the reformed Indo-Aryan religion obtained preferance - Prehistoric ancient and Hindu India, p.88, R.D. Banerji.
With Buddhism dawned a new era in the history of India. Buddhism arose as a revolt against the tyranny of the priests who were Brahmanas. Brahmanism in its later stages had assumed very arrogant air. 1. The Vedanta was a great reformation which began at least four centuries B.C. when Buddhism had obtained a firm hold in upper India ... It is clearly a Dravidian reformation of the crude Aryan elemental teaching, a building up of a new-Hinduism purified by the ancient Turano philosophic schools of Kapila and embracing the piety and ethics of the followers of the great Jaina saint Mahavira and his probable disciple Sakya Muni-Short studies in the science of comparative religions, p.265.
1. Maya is the power which enables him to produce mutable nature. It is sakti, or the energy of Iswara, or atmaviriti, the power of self-becoming. Iswara and maya in this sense are mutually dependent and are both beginingless. The power of the supreme is called maya in the Gita. Since the Lord is able to produce the universe by means of the two elements of his being, prakriti and purusa, matter and consciousness, they are said to be higher and lower of god. Gradually, Maya becomes to mean the lower prakriti, since Purusa is said to be the seed which the Lord casts into the womb of prakriti for the germination of the universe - Indian philosophy, vol.I, p.547 Radhakrishnan.

Siva is a god unknown to the Vedas; his name is a word of not frequent occurrence in hymns, indeed, but means simply ‘prosperous’; not even in the Atharvan it is the epithet of a particular divinity, or distinguished by the useage from any other adjectives. The precise relation between Siva and Rudra is not yet satisfactorily traced out - Orient and linguistic studies, p.30 - William Dwlight Whitney.
It is an established fact that the god Siva was the form which the Vedic god Rudra later assumed. In other words the god Siva, at least as he has been described in classical times, was unknown to the Vedas, and Rudra the Tempest God of the Vedas is not given any of the distinctive epithets which later came to be associated with the god Siva. If we accept the alleged identification we have to date the god Siva or his proto type in the middle of the third millenium B.C. For, that is the date of the Mohenjo-Daro finds, as has been proved by Professor Selon Lloyd on the strength of the happy discovery of the cylindrical seal at Tel-as-mar which contains a representation of a typically mohenjo-Daro scene-an Indian elephant, rhinoceros and a crocodile. Identification of Mohenjo-Daro figure-B.A. Saletore-New review X, July - Dec. 1939.
Now it seems possible that Rudra in the Rig-Veda was an Aryanised form from the pre-Aryan proto-Siva. This supposition to a certain extent finds support in the fact that the word Rudra in Sanskrit meaning ‘Red’ is identical with Dravidian word ‘red’ Siva, Rudra, it must be noted, was not a very important deity in the Rig-Veda. Only three hymns have been given to him, and he is identified with Agni. It seems probable that these pre-Aryan phallic worshippers are identical with the people who in later times dwelt in rich and prosperous cities in the Indus valley, and prejudice and indignation against whom find most eloquent expression in the following two passages of the Rig-Veda ... The cult of linga in three faced Siva is common among represen-
tations of Siva. It is ordinarily Agamic principle that Siva in his aspect of Maheswara or Sadasiva can be represented with one, three, four or five faces but not with two. But the fact is there, the image represented with three faces and other associations are clearly Saivaic in character. The conclusion there fore seems to be thoroughly justified that it is the figure of Siva that is represented on this. This would only be confirmed by the yogic posture of Siva in one aspect is represented as Mahayoge and sometimes called Yoge - Daks hanamurthi. In such, his associations are naturally with the forest and the surrounding elements indicated in the picture are sylvan life ... 1. From the identification of Chandragupta Maurya to the excavations of Mohenjo Daro and Harappa, from the deciphering of the inscriptions of Asoka to the comparative survey of epigraphic records over India, the material for the writing of Indian history was provided by the work of European scholars. Even more striking is the case of Indonesia, where few European scholars, mostly Dutch reconstructed from inscriptions the history of the great empires of Java and Sumatra which provided Indonesian nationalism with a solid historical basis. In this sense it cannot be denied that European scholars and thinkers, by their labour in the interest of knowlge, enabled India, Ceylon and Indonesia to think on terms of historical continuity.

* The early Vedic religion was a cult of magic, a system of propitation or constraint of Nature-powers (Devas) by means of sacrifices (Yajnas), offerings of animal fat, (ghee vapa, etc) and fermented liquor (Soma) poured into fire regarded as the mouth of the Gods, and accompanied with the chanting of mantras. Some of these mantras were incantations of praise, and others combinations of sounds having no meaning, being sometimes inarticulate cries (“like the bellowing of a bull etc.”) They were believed to please or constrain the Devas and thus to secure the fulfilment of the sacrificers desires, whether these were the acquisition of material objects in this life or the enjoyment of pleasures in post-mortem states. - Outlines of Indian Philosophy p.118.

* They were translated from Sanskrit into Persian by or for Dara Shukoh, the eldest son of the Mugal emperor Shah Jehan who held the liberal religious views of Akbar. He had heard of the Upanishads in Kashmir in 1640 invited several Pandits to Delhi to assist in their translation and finished the work in 1657. Translated into Persian then the most widely read language of the East, they became generally accessible. In 1775 a manuscript of this Persian translation was sent by the French resident at the court of Shujaud Daula to Anquetil Duperron the discoverer of the Avesta; and later another manuscript. Anquetil Duperron collected the two and translated the work into French and into Latin publishing the latter version in 1801 and 1802 under the title of Oupnekhat a corruption of upanishad. This Latin translation was studied by Schopenhaner. Twelve of them are translated by Maxmuller with introduction and notes in the “Sacred books of the East”. - The century cyclopaedia of names.

# The ethical end of the Sankhya system is to effect the liberation of the purusha or soul from the fetters in which it is evolved by union with Prakriti. The Sankhya proper not so much denies the existence of supreme being as ignores it as incapable of
dialectical demonstration. “He must be free from desires and not bound by troubles. If he were bound by desires of any kind he would be under bondage and deficient in power”. - The Century Cyclopaedia of Names.

* Vedanta - The most Common designation of the Uttaramimamsa school of Hindu philosophy given to it either as teaching the ultimate aim of Veda or as founded on the Upanishads, came at the end of the Veda as the last stage in its historic evolution. It is ascribed to Vyasa or Badarayana. The first of the names (‘arranger’) is also given to the legendary person who is supposed to have arranged the Vedas and written the Mahabharata, Puranas and Dharmasastra and was doubtless applied to various great writers or compliers as a kind of title. In this sense it seems to have been given to the founder of the Vedanta. Its principles are propounded in Sutras, but Badarayana’s Sutras are generally called Brahmasutras or sometimes Sharirakasutra. The text of the celebrated commentary of Sankaracharya have been edited in the “Bibliotheca Indica” and a portion translated, and also the commentary known as Vedanta Sara. The most authoritative recent works on the Vedanta are however paul Deussen’s “Die Sutras des Vedanta” - The Century Cyclopaedia of Names.

# Smartas: Smarta Brahmins - one of the three principal classes into which the Hindus proper of the present day may be divided as to religion, the other two being the Saivas and the Vaisnavas. The Smarta believe that the man’s spirit is identical with the one spirit which is the essence of the universe and only cognizable through the three personal gods Brahma, Shiva and Vishnu with their subordinate dieties but only as co-equal manifestations of one impersonal spirit and as destined to be reabsorbed into the spirit. They are followers of Sankara - The Century Cyclopaedia of Names.

* Puranas - The name of each of a class of Sanskrit works important in their connection with the later phases of Brahmanism, as exhibited in the doctrines of emanation, incarnation and triple manifestation. They are the Vedas of popular Hinduism and contain the history of the Gods, interwoven with every variety of legendary tradition on other subjects. Though nominally tritheistic, they are practically polytheistic and essentially pantheistic. Their form is in general that of dialogues in which a well known sage answers the questions of his disciples, while others are monologues. They are written in sloka matter of the Mahabharata, with occassional passages in prose. They are 18 in number. There are also 18 Upapuranas or Subordinate Puranas
- The Century Cyclopaedia of Names.

* The Dharma Sutras were manuals written by the teachers of the Vedic Schools for the guidance of their pupils. Their use was therefore, at first restricted to these schools alone and it was not till a later period that they were acknowledged as authority all over India. The Smirthis on the other hand were declared to be of divine origin and hence claimed from the very beginning to be authentic sources of law for all Aryans - “The History and Culture of the Indian People - Vol.II p.225.”

* No.99 in vol.ii. part V. of South Indian inscriptions gives an interesting account of a gift of a village for the purpose of supporting 308 learned Brahmans in persuit of their sacred vocations of studying and teaching as prescribed in the Sastras. Regarding the qualifications of the select body of Brahman scholars it is stated in the inscription that they had all studied the three Vedas and Smiritis. The inscription applies to them various learned designations such as Cathurvedin, Triveden, Somajajin, Sadangavid, Bhatta, Kramavid (proficient in the Krama - patha of the Rig Veda & C.)
A similar gift for establishing a similar colony of 308 Brahmans is also Registered in No.7 of 1912 No.277 of 1913 refers to the establishment of another cultured colony of 108 Brahman families equipped with all necessaries of life and even with library called Saraswathi Bhandara. No.278 of 1913 registers a similar grant for the same number of Brahman colonists. No.198 of 1919 records the interesting case of an assembly holding a special meeting in response to a royal order which requested them to adjudge the merits of a literary work composed by a poet. The work was recited before the assembly and the author obtained as a reward for his labours a grant of land to be held in perpetual ownership. Students of Tamil literature may find here a lingering literary tradition of the more ancient Dravidian Sangam established in Madura to scrutinze
the works of Tamil poets and advance the cause of Tamil literature (mid. Ep. Rep. for 1919. p.98) - Local Government in Ancient India p.283. Radhakumud Mookerji M.A. Ph.D.
# Gradually the Dravidians adopted Aryan manners customs and religion. The Dravidian priests became Brahmanas and the kings of all tribes claimed to be Kshatriyas - Junior History of India p.17 R.D. Banerji.
* The Agamas represent the oldest products of Dravidian literature, that in prehistoric times they were written in the Dravidian (Tamil) language, and a great part of them was lost in a flood which swept over the land south of the present Cape Comorin, the chief dwelling place of the old Dravidians. Only remnants of the older Agamas were translated into Sanskrit and preserved in this form. But as has been urged, all that one can say is that the home of the Agamas was in the land of the Dravidians i.e. the south of India. From the south they seem to have pushed up north, and later to have turned back to the south where they helped to drive out Jainsm and Buddhism. It has been further said that should one incline towards the theory that Agama literature was of Dravidian origin, one must at the same time admit that it came under the influence of Sanskrit literature very early. What is preserved to us of the Agamas bears unmistakably the stamp of Sanskrit literature, for the Agamas that are preserved are in the Sanskrit language, and the systems based in the Agama and written in the non-Sanskrit language employ Sanskrit terms so that as matters now stand, we have to consider the Agama literature as a part of the Sanskrit literature - The Saiva Siddhanta in the Meykanda Sastra - Violet Paranjothi M.A.L.T.Ph.D. (Isabella Thouburn College, Lucknow - 1938) quoted as an English translation from Der Saiva Siddhanta, a German book by H.W. * The Vedic culture which resembles that of the Homeric Greeks or the Celtic Irish at the beginning of the Christian era, or that of the pre-Christian Teutans and Slaves becomes transformed in the epics into the Hindu culture through the influence of Dravidians. The Aryan idea of worship during the earliest period was to call on the Father sky or some other shining one to look from on high on the sacrificer and receive from him the offerings of fat or flesh, cakes and drink. But soon puja or worship takes the place of Homa or sacrifice. Image worship which was a striking feature of the Dravidian faith was accepted by the Aryans. The ideals of vegetarianism and non-violence (ahimsa) also developed. The Vedic tradition has dominated by the Agamic and today Hindu culture shows the influences of the Agama as much as that of the Vedas. The Aryan and the Dravidian do not exist side by side in Hinduism. “contact with the highly civilized Dravidians led to the transformation of Vedism into theistic religion.” - Hindu view in life - Dr.S.Radhakrishnan.

1. Many other nations mention, in the mythological part of their history, in undations which in their essential particulars, agree with the scriptural account of Noah’s preservation. Hence many persons have inferred the universality of this inundation. To this it has been replied that each nation localizes the chief events and actors as connected with itself, necessitating an Ararat, an ark and a Noah in each instance. Fohi in the Chinese mythology, Satyavrata in the Indian, Xisuthrus in the Chaldaean, Ogyges and Deucation in t he Greek, have each been recognised by many as the Noah of the sacred scripture under different names. Even the American Indians have a tradition of a similar deluge, and a renewal of the race from the family of one individual. All these individuals are said be their respective nation to have been saved , and to have become the father of mankind.’ - A New Popular Encyclopaedia Vol.IV p.325.

Now the sun in the course of the year travels through the constellations of the Zodiac, which were called houses. Accordingly each month of the sun being in a different house was supposed to take a different form and since the constellations of the Poto - Indians as said above were only eight, the forms of the sun i.e., the Supreme Being were eight. The eight forms of the Supreme Being were the eight constellations which were the following: The Ram, the Harp, the Crab, the Mother, the Scale, the Arrow, the Jar and the Fish or the two Fishes. Images of the supreme being under these forms were worshipped in different parts of the country. The most popular of these forms of God, seem to have been the Fish. Ophiolatria, the worship of the serpent next to the adoration of the Phallus , is one of the most remarkable and at first sight unaccountable forms of religions the world has ever known. Until the true source from whence it sprung can be reached and understood, its nature will remain at mysterious as its universality, for what man could see in an object so repulsive and forbidding in its habits, as this reptile, to render worship to its one of the most difficult of problems to find a solution to. There is hardly a country of the ancient world, however where it cannot be traced pervading every known system of mythology, and having proofs of its existence and extant in the shape of monuments, temples and earthworks of the most elaborate and curious character. Babylon, Persia, Hindustan, Ceylon, China, Japan, Burmah, Java, Arabia, Syria, Asiya minor, Egypt, Ethiopia, Greece, Italy, North and Western Europe, Mexico,
Peru, America all yeild abundant testimony to the same effect and point to the common origin of Pagan system wherever found Ophiolatria - p.1.

1. Horned Gods were common in Mesopotamia, both in Babylon and Assyria. The great Gods and Goddesses had seven horns, which is the reason that the divine lamb in the book of revelation was said to have seven horns ... The horns were a sign of divinity. When king or high priest appeared as the God Asshur with the queen or high priestess as his consort Ishtar, the appropriate number of horns was worn on the royal pair being then regarded as the incarnat e deities. When Alexander the Great raised himself above the king of the earth and made himself a God, he wore horns in sign of his divinity hence his name in the Koran Dhu’l Karnan, the two horned ... The Indian figures of the horned Gods found at Mohenjo - Daro, are of the earliest bronze - age. The most remarkable is that of a man with bull’s horns on his head sitting crosslegged, surrounded with animals the representative was regarded in historic times as a form of Siva and is called Pasupathi ... When in relief sculpture Pasupathi is three faced, as here; but in figures in the round he has four faces. Such a representation in a native attempt to show the all seeing God, as is found in Europe in the four faced of Janus. It is still uncertain whether the four faced form arose independently in India and Europe, or whether one is the prototype of the other if the later, the India appears to be the earlier - The God of the witches p. 15 - Margret Allice Murray.

“The beared God who grasping a trident in his extended left hands heads, the procession of male figures is probably the father deity. The great Hittite God
of thundering sky, whose emblems were the thunderbolt and the bull; for the trident which he carries may resonably be interpreted as thunderbolt. The deity is represented in two stone monuments of Hittite art which were found at Zenjirli in Northern Syria and Bobylonia repectively. On both we see a male God wearing the usual Hittite costume of tall cap, short tunic, and shoes turned up to the toes, a crescent hilted sword in girt at his side; his hands are raised in the right, he holds a single headed axe or hammar, in his left a trident of wavy lines, which is thought to stand for forked lightning or a bundle of thunderbolts. On the Babylonian slab which bears a long Hittite inscription the God’s cap is ornamented with a pair of horns. The horns on the cap are probably those of a bull; for in another Hittite monument found at Malatia on the Euphrates there is carried a deity on the usual Hittite costume standing on a bull grasping a trident or thunderbolt in his left hand, while facing him stands a priest clothed in long robe holding a crook or curved staff in one hand and pouring a libation with the other.” 
In the sculpture the God on the bull holds in his right hand what is discribed as a triangular bow instead of a mace or an axe or a hammer. The Hittite Thunder God also is known to us from a treaty of alliance which about the year 1290 B.C. was contracted between Huttusil, King of Hittites and Remeses II, King of Egypt. By a singular piece of good fortune we possess copies of this treaty both in Hittite and in Egyptian languages. The Hittite copy was found some years ago inscribed in cuniform characters in a clay tablet at Borgazkeni; the copies of the treaty of Egyptian language are engraved on the walls of the temples of Thebes. From the Egyptian copies which have been read and translated, we gather that the sun God was principal deity, of the Hittites and the Hittite scales which appended to the treaty exhibited the king embraced by the Thunder - God and the queen embraced the sun goddess Arenna. The Hittite divinity of thundering sky appears to have long survived at Doliche in Commagene, forin late Roman art he reappears under the title of Jupiter. Dolichenus wearing a phrygian cap, standing on a bull and weilding double axe in one hand and a thunder bolt in the other. In this form his worship was transported from the native Syrian home by soldiers and slaves, till it had
spread over a large part of the Roman Empire especially in the frontiers, while it flourished in the camps of the legions. The combination of the bull with the thunderbolt as emblems of the deity suggests that the animal may have been chosen to represent the sky God not merely of its virility but of its voice; for in the peal of thunder primitive man may well have heard the bellowing of a celestial bull.

1. The theory and practice of yoga are entirely foreign to the trend of early and later Vedic religious thoughts and inclinations. It has now been definitely shown by Mr. Chanda with the help of some Mohenjo - Daro sculptures that the idea can be traced to Indus people. It is but natural that the people should have attributed to their God all the characteristics of a yogie including austerities and self - mortification. It is common to believe that the creator himself must perform austerities in order to aualify himself for the capacity of creating manthought Gods, in his own light; process which could bring destruction on man must have been gone thoroughly by Gods to attain their exalted position. It must have been such a belief which led the Indus people to conceive of and depict their God as a meditator.
The intimate connection between Samkhya and yoga are too well known to require repetition. The philosophy of the yoga system may be regarded as practically the same as that of the Samkhya with conception of a personal God super imposed upon it. It therefore appears certain that Samkhya too, which orthodox Hindu opinion has regarded as non-Vedic in character, was, like yoga, a system of thought which had a pre-Vedic origin.
It has been suspected for a long time by scholars that some non-Aryan tracts are contained in the later-day. Siva worship the tract assumption that everything. Aryan must have been nobler than and superior to the non-Aryan led them to think that the uncanny features which the worship involves, could not have come out of the Aryan religion without the impact of some alien ideas.
But so long there was no evidence to lend force to the conjecture or to asce rtain what was the nature of the Aryan influences - Indian Culture - Vol.II - Siva, His Pre-Aryan Origins - Amalananda Ghosh.
1. The word Sambu - as a Vedic epithet, is well known to be derived from Sam; blessing, welfare, prosperity plus the radical bhu; ‘be, become and to mean’ being a blessing beneficient as a name in later times, of Siva. I feel that it is likely to have been chosen because it suggested in the minds of the speakers some Dravidian word akin to the Tamil Cem, ‘redness’ (of Tamil cempoo ‘copper’) the colour red being always associated with this deity. That is to say, the application of the epithet to Siva - seems to me to become more intelligible under the above assumption of the existence in northern India at an early period of a race or races related to the Dravidians of the South, Sambu as a name of Siva becomes in Tamil Campu which, if an early importation, would as I argue, have been originally pronounced with an initial sound like that of the English Church. I venture the suggestion that this word has reverted to Sanskrit from some Dravidic dialect in the form of Jambu, as a name of Siva bearing the connection of ‘reddishness’. Both Jambuka and Siva are used to denote a jackal, possibly because of the tawny colour of the animal and when it is considered that the area characterized pre-eminently by the worship of Siva must have been originally south of the zone into which Aryan civilization had advanced, it will not, I think, be felt to be impossible that it was to this unkown region that the expression Jambu-dvipa, ‘the Siva-country first had a reference - Sanskrit Element in the Vocabularies of the Dravidian Languages pp.61,62 - Remarks by M.Collins.
